speechtext:
There have been four progress reports. As hon. members know, the practice of the international joint commission is to make only one final report containing recommendations to the two governments. That is their function, and then it is the responsibility

Manitoba Flood
of the two governments to decide whether or not they shall act on the report. So far it has always been possible for the two sections of the international joint commission to make the same report, and I think it is correct to say that the reports have always been acted upon by the two governments.
It is not the practice of the international joint commission to make available, either to the governments or to the public, working papers and material upon which the commission arrives at its decision and recommendations; therefore it has never been the practice to table reports of this kind, and I understand that that will not be done in this case.
Perhaps at this time I might also deal with the motion standing in the name of the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) for the production of papers. The reference in this case was made by letter dated January 12, 1948. It is not usual for the governments to communicate with the commission, which is the instrument of both governments, after a reference has been made. But in this case the course was adopted, as has been reported already to the house, of communicating with the commission, and a letter was sent to the chairman of the Canadian section by myself as Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs under date of May 18, 1950. speechtext: I take it from what the Acting Minister of External Affairs has said about tabling this information that there will be no objection to one or more members of the international joint commission appearing before the special committee on external affairs?

subtopic: RED RIVER VALLEY
subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO INTER- NATIONAL JOINT COMMISSION
speechtext:
I can assure my hon. friend that his assumption is certainly not correct. In the view of those with whom I have had an opportunity of discussing the matter, it would be quite improper for any member of the international joint commission or one of its officials to appear before a committee of parliament to discuss a matter which is still in process of consideration. After the international joint commission has arrived at a decision and made its recommendations to the governments, the situation might be different; but until the commission, which is representative of both countries, has had an opportunity to consider all the information before it and arrive at a decision, it would not be proper for a member of the commission to appear before a committee of this house for the purpose of stating views and expressing opinions before even his col-
leagues on the other section, or perhaps on the Canadian section itself, had had an opportunity of considering the position.
I suggest that that would end the usefulness of the commission as an international organization which has been remarkably successful and which has presented an example to the whole world of the way in which two countries can co-operate. One of the secrets of its success has been the fact that it has been objectively representative of both countries, and that its recommendations have always been carried out.

maintopic: HON. LIAQUAT ALI KHAN   VISIT OF PRIME MINISTER OF PAKISTAN-INQUIRY AS TO ARRANGEMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is understood that the Prime Minister of Pakistan will arrive from Boston at Rockcliffe airport, Ottawa, at 11 a.m. on Tuesday, May 30. He will be greeted by a general salute by the guard of honour, and at 12.30 will lay a wreath at the national war memorial. That evening he will be entertained by Their Excellencies. At 11.00 a.m. on Wednesday, May 31, he will confer with members of the cabinet. I am informed that the Prime Minister has already approached the Speaker of this house and the Speaker of the Senate for the purpose of arranging, if it meets the wishes of all hon. members, for the Prime Minister of Pakistan to address a joint meeting of both houses at 3 p.m. on Wednesday, May 31, in accordance with the practice under which prime ministers of commonwealth countries have been extended that invitation. There will be a government dinner that night.
On Friday', June 2, the Prime Minister of Pakistan will leave by air for Kingston, where he will be received by the national conference of Canadian universities and the members of the national defence college. That same day he will proceed by air to Toronto where he will visit the international trade fair. Later he will leave Toronto by automobile for Niagara Falls, where he will spend the night and stay until he leaves Canadian soil on Saturday afternoon.

subtopic: TRIBUTES AND EXPRESSIONS OF SYMPATHY
speechtext:
Before we proceed to the orders of the day I would deem it a privilege, Mr. Speaker, if I might make a reference to the passing of a great soldier, a wonderful administrator and a constructive statesman who was a personal acquaintance of mine. I refer, of course, to the late Field Marshal Wavell. He would not be known to many Canadian soldiers during the first world war, but between the first and second world wars his name became known to a great many Canadians in the different services, because he had prepared a textbook on the campaigns in the Near East which gave an outline of the type of operation in which Canadians were to take part in the second world war. In addition, his series of lectures on generals and generalship showed not only that he was preparing himself for high command but that he was indicating a way to leadership which was followed by a great many Canadians in the second world war.
I became acquainted with the late field marshal when he was in command of the second division at Aldershot during the thirties. There his original methods of training and instilling initiative into the British soldier were the forerunners of the battle drills which were later associated with Field Marshal Montgomery.
During the second world war, of course, he was in command in Africa and the Middle East. There, with very slender resources, he was able to make use of his great business capacity in organizing for victory in Africa in 1940. His supreme moment of trial, and I think the greatest triumph of his life, came when he was called upon to implement the decision of the allies to support Greece from

Aeronautics Act
the few resources he had available. His decision in that respect has been frequently criticized; but a given pledge was kept and a nation's honour saved, two matters which were of no small importance to a man of Earl Wavell's character.
I think every Canadian of Hellenic extraction will feel that he has lost a true friend in the passing of Field Marshal Wavell, and I am sure this house and everyone concerned extends deepest sympathy to Lady Wavell and her family.

speakeroldname: Hon. Brooke Claxion (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: TRIBUTES AND EXPRESSIONS OF SYMPATHY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, because I had already sent messages to Lady Wavell and to Mr. Shinwell, Secretary of State for War in the United Kingdom, it had not been my intention to make reference today to the death of this great soldier. However, I should like to associate myself with everything that has been said by the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes).
It was not my privilege to know Viscount Wavell through having served under or with him, as it was the privilege of the hon. member for Nanaimo, but I think we were fortunate in that it was possible for him to visit Canada last November in his capacity as honorary colonel of the Black Watch, Royal Highland Regiment of Montreal, and on that occasion he visited a number of our defence establishments, including the national defence college and Royal Military College. He showed himself to be an understanding leader as well as a great soldier, and when he died I am sure many of us had the feeling that we had lost a firm friend of our country and of our services.

Then clauses 4 to 9 of the bill deal with the air transport board, which was set up under part II of the Aeronautics Act passed in 1944. The effect of the amendments is to form a board of three, a chairman and two members, who will administer the Aeronautics Act, take over the duties now being performed by the board of transport commissioners in regulating civil aviation as well as the duty of assigning airworthiness certificates and of licensing aviation enterprises within Canada. In addition, the board will function to advise the government as to ways and means of advancing civil aviation. The board will take the initiative in laying out routes, within Canada and overseas, which promise possibilities of profitable operation and will guide the government in seeing that these routes are operated by Canadians who are capable of carrying out such undertakings.
The judicial functions of the board are not new, but the functions of the board as advisers to the government on aviation policy are new, and will, I think, be helpful in bringing about the rapid development of civil aviation, both internal and external.
Members will notice that at that time the minister, who was then minister of munitions and supply, attributed great importance to this air transport board. In the committee the other day we got a short statement from the chairman of the board indicating just what it is doing at the present time, six years after that statement. The statement of the chairman of the board will be found at page 243 of the minutes of proceedings and evidence of that committee. He was asked what the functions of the board now are, and this is his answer:
The board under the minister is responsible for the granting of licences or refusal of licences, as the case may be, to commercial air services.
Members will note those words, "under the minister". That is the first job of the board, and here is the second:
It is also responsible for general economic regulation and economic relationships between commercial air services-
Then, the third is:
-and for such general aviation matters as the minister wishes the board to report upon or offer advice upon.
The fourth and final job of the air transport board is indicated by the following statement of its chairman:
Apart from that I should also add it is responsible on behalf of the government for taking care of the policy matters in connection with our part in the International Civil Aviation Organization, and the Canadian representative on the council of ICAO is a member of the board's staff.

Aeronautics Act

speechtext: This is a general discussion I am engaging in now.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO POWER OF MINISTER TO MAKE REGULATIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Proceed, and I shall see.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO POWER OF MINISTER TO MAKE REGULATIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
The air transport board, in
dealing with applications for licences, which is their first function, should be able to act as a judicial body, free and independent of interference of any kind by the minister or any other authority. That is the position of the board of transport commissioners when they deal with applications having to do with the railways of Canada or with shipping, or when they act under the other powers conferred upon them.
The Aeronautics Act provides that the air transport board, in issuing a licence, must be satisfied that the proposed service is and will be required by the present and future public convenience and necessity of Canada; in other words, in the Aeronautics Act they are given that test-the consideration must be the public convenience and necessity. Furthermore, in the amendments which were passed to the Aeronautics Act in 1945, the air transport board were given the power of a court; for example, they have powers to have their orders enforced in certain courts of the land; they have power to send for witnesses, and they have power to issue commissions to take evidence; they are given wide powers, just as though they were an independent court; but actually their position is not that at all.
In the committee we questioned the chairman of the air transport board about the powers of the board in issuing a licence, and about the control the Minister of Transport had or has over these applications. At page 244 of the minutes of proceedings and evidence we find the following:
Q. When you render a decision -
That is, on an application for a licence.
-is that published by yourselves and a licence issued, or do you merely recommend it to the minister?
A. The board's decision is signed by the board members and if it is an affirmative decision it is submitted to the minister for his approval; if he approves the decision he signs it and the board then issues a licence to the carrier. In the event of a denial of an application, that under the statute may be taken care of by the board itself without submission to the minister, but with the right of appeal on the part of the carrier to the minister.
Then I asked him this question:
Q. I see. So that if an application is granted you make a recommendation, and then that has to be approved by the Minister of Transport?
A. That is correct.
Q. And, subject to that approval, you issue the licence?
A. That is correct.
[The Chairman.]
Q. And if the application is denied there is no recommendation made by the board to the minister but the applicant has the right of appeal to the minister?
A. The applicant has the right of appeal to the minister.
Q. Is that appeal to the minister or to the cabinet?
A. To the minister.
There are hundreds of applications for these licences. Here we have the position that this air transport board, which was set up by the present Minister of Trade and Commerce in 1944 with such a glowing description of the part it was to be allowed to play in aviation, has no power to issue a single licence without having the application referred to the Minister of Transport. The jurisdiction of the board of transport commissioners is, of course, quite different. It is a judicial body; it makes its decision and the only appeal is to the governor in council. But this air transport board is handicapped in that,, in every case in which an application is granted, it can only recommend to the minister, and he has the final approval or rejection of that application.
That provision, Mr. Chairman, has two bad results. In the first place, it must of necessity weaken the air transport board, and anything that tends to weaken it is a bad thing. This air transport board should be made into a strong body. The second bad effect is that the Minister of Transport is given too much power. He is not in a position to know whether or not those applications should be granted. How on earth is it possible for him to judge the merits of hundreds of applications for licences? It simply is not possible for him to do that, and I do not believe he does it. I think he just takes the recommendation of the air transport board and approves of the granting of the licence. That very fact is clear proof that this power of the minister should be done away with and that the air transport board should have the final word as to whether or not an application for a licence is to be granted. There would have to be some appeal, of course; but if there is to be an appeal, then let that appeal be to the cabinet.
This power held by the Minister of Transport over the issuing of licences is a hangover from the days when the present Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) was administering the act. He likes to have powers of that kind right in his hands, and the air transport board was set up with that idea in mind; it was set up so that it could not make a move without coming to him. He had an arbitrary and dictatorial control over the air transport board. In my opinion the time

has come when that control should be done away with. There may have been some excuse for it during the war-

speechtext:
I do not know what that has to do with the debate. Now that the Minister of Labour has had his little say, perhaps we can get back to the Minister of Transport.
I was saying that this dictatorial power is a hangover from the days when the present Minister of Trade and Commerce was the minister in charge, and that it should be wiped out. There is now no reason why the minister should have a veto over every decision made by the air transport board on an application for a licence.
The air transport board is working under another handicap. When the board was set up in 1944 a provision was written into the act to the effect that the board could not issue a licence to anyone in the transportation business without such applicant first obtaining the approval of the governor in council. That meant that the air transport board could not issue a licence to a shipping company to go into the air transport business, or to a trucking company. The restrictions covered all other forms of transportation business.
Aeronautics Act
The reason was that at that time the present Minister of Trade and Commerce had a battle on with the Canadian Pacific Railway, and had announced as his policy that they would have to divest themselves of Canadian Pacific Air Lines-and, incidentally, that the Canadian National Railways had to get rid of their interest in Trans-Canada Air Lines. That was the policy at the time the air transport board was set up in 1944.
However, the provision is still in the act. It is another hangover from those days when the present Minister of Trade and Commerce was in charge. Government policy has now changed. The Canadian Pacific Railway have been allowed to carry on and greatly to extend Canadian Pacific Air Lines. Canadian National Railways have been allowed to retain their ownership of Trans-Canada Air Lines. But, while the policy has been changed, the air transport board still labours under these restrictions.
We asked the chairman of the board about it, and this is what he said as it is reported at page 272 of the proceedings of the committee:

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO POWER OF MINISTER TO MAKE REGULATIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Green, I believe the original
statutory restriction in this regard appears because it was felt that some such precaution was required to ensure the fullest possible development of commercial aviation. The reason for that was that it might be possible for a surface carrier to acquire control of an air service which was competitive with it for the deliberate purpose of stifling the air service. That was the fundamental reasoning behind the original restriction, as I understand it, and I do not know that there is much more that I can offer in the way of explanation other than to say that there are alternative methods of taking care of that situation. One of them is the method which parliament took of writing this restriction into the act leaving a way open for exceptions where no harm was going to result. Alternatively-
And I draw attention to this alternative.
-it could be dealt with through the control of licensing but it seems to me that the alternative selected is not a matter for the board to decide but for the government and parliament to decide upon.
And the chairman of the board was quite right in taking that stand. In effect he said, "I cannot do anything about this; it is up to-the government". I do suggest the air transport board should not be asked to work under that further restriction.
Then a further restriction is placed on the board by the government. This is what I call the monopoly policy of the government, in so far as aviation is concerned. A discussion of this subject appears at page 251 of the proceedings of the committee, where I questioned Mr. Baldwin as follows;
Q. What is the policy of the board with regard to the control of competition? I understand that you are pretty strict about lines competing on routes.

Aeronautics Act
Does that mean that you decide that one line shall have a monopoly on a route; or, just what does it mean?
A. The policy of the government, as you will recollect, was laid down some time ago to the effect that not more than one "scheduled" air line, to make that distinction, should operate on any one route, and the board has operated within the framework of that general policy in that where we have found that public convenience and necessity require the provision of a scheduled air service only one operator is licensed to perform that service.
Then later on he referred to the non-sched-uled field in this way:
When you come to the non-scheduled field the policy is somewhat different. We use our discretion in granting to what we call class two routes which are services on an irregular basis following a regular route pattern. Normally speaking we have only had one carrier on a class two route for the simple reason that we have followed the philosophy which governed the decision regarding scheduled operators.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO POWER OF MINISTER TO MAKE REGULATIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Would you read the next sentence, please?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO POWER OF MINISTER TO MAKE REGULATIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Yes.
The factor which governs in a situation of this kind is the potential traffic which exists in Canada, and generally it has not been sufficient to justify putting on more than one carrier; otherwise neither would have a chance to succeed.
The point I make is this: Surely if the board is competent, then it should be given full responsibility, without being hedged in by these different restrictions from the government. Furthermore, it has no control whatever over Trans-Canada Air Lines. That provision was set out in the amendment to the Aeronautics Act of 1944, and there is a further amendment in the present bill.
The chairman explained quite clearly just what the position of the board is in connection with Trans-Canada Air Lines. The questions and answers in this connection are found at page 252, as follows:
Q. What control does the board have over Trans-Canada Air Lines?
A. The board is required to grant licences to Trans-Canada Air Lines in accordance with contracts that may be approved between the government and Trans-Canada Air Lines. That having been done. Trans-Canada Air Lines comes within the general rate jurisdiction of the board; and as far as direct control in regard to their licensing goes we exercise no independent jurisdiction. We may be called upon to advise the government with regard to a proposed T.C.A. service, but once a contract is authorized by the government then we are required by statute to grant a licence.
Q. In effect then the operations of T.C.A. are outside of your scope and you have to issue permits for them to fly a route if they apply for it?
A. Except in so far as the period during which the route is being discussed in the first instance is concerned; that is, before the government reaches a decision to operate a certain route; and the practice is that the board is called upon to advise the government as to whether it is a route which the government should designate for operation by T.C.A.

Q. And the T.C.A. routes are designated by the government?
A. That is correct.
Q. And once that has been done the board has no jurisdiction?
A. The situation is virtually the same as when an international agreement authorizing routes is made. In the first instance our role is advisory and in negotiating, but once the decision is made by the government we carry it out.
Q. Which means that you really have no licensing authority in the international field, you act only in an advisory capacity?
A. That is correct, sir.
There again we have the situation where the board is not free to deal, on its merits, with an application by Trans-Canada Air Lines for a licence. They must accept the route dictated by the government. I believe the present Minister of Trade and Commerce said in one of the other committees of the house the other day that he is the man who decides what routes should be flown by T.C.A. So it is not even the Minister of Transport who has that degree of jurisdiction. Here we find an outside minister deciding on the routes and the air transport board really has no discretion or authority whatsoever. .
It will be noticed that the chairman said the same was true in connection with international air routes. In effect, the air transport board has no authority over international routes; and the bill before the committee today cuts down the statutory authority the board formerly had in that respect. I believe further that the air transport board will have practically no authority with regard to non-scheduled international services. The other day the minister did not set out government policy with regard to these services. He promised to give us order 15, I think it was, which sets out the powers.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO POWER OF MINISTER TO MAKE REGULATIONS, ETC.
speechtext: I have it here.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO POWER OF MINISTER TO MAKE REGULATIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
We have not received it as yet but I take it from the evidence given by Mr. Baldwin, chairman of the air transport board, that that board will have little authority with regard to international non-scheduled air services. Incidentally it was agreed that these services were becoming of greater importance all the time.
The board has no control whatsoever over private aircraft. I do not know whether it would be possible to give them some authority over private aircraft, but it seems to me-I am not speaking as an expert-that the air transport board should have some control over such aircraft.
That is just a summary of the handicaps under which the air transport board is working. I believe that hon. members generally would prefer to see this board given real authority so that it could carry on as the

present Minister of Trade and Commerce indicated in 1944. Then, the plan was that the air transport board would give leadership in promoting civil aviation in Canada. I do not believe that the board is in position to do that today because of the various restrictions I have mentioned. I do hope that the minister will not be too abrupt in turning down these suggestions or saying that the board has all the authority it needs.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO POWER OF MINISTER TO MAKE REGULATIONS, ETC.
speechtext: He never is.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO POWER OF MINISTER TO MAKE REGULATIONS, ETC.
speechtext: No. I must admit that he is not as abrupt as some other ministers. These suggestions are placed before him and before the committee with great earnestness, believing that we could further the development of civil aviation in Canada if the air transport board was given additional authority.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO POWER OF MINISTER TO MAKE REGULATIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
The remarks I wish to make I intended to defer until a later section of the bill is before us, but because of what the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra has said perhaps I should say something at this point. I sympathize with the view of the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra that the air transport board seems to be getting into a position where its functions are merely perfunctory. However, I must part company with the hon. member when he suggests that the air transport board somehow or other should be divorced completely from government direction and government policy.
My mind goes back to 1944 when this act in its present form was introduced. The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra and I were both here and we took part in the debate- on opposite sides. It seems to me that there are things that are natural monopolies, such as railroads, electrical services and pipe lines if you will. In certain cases it is not in the public interest to have two lines where one will do the job. In connection with public services, public utilities and natural monopolies of this kind, either there should be complete public ownership or the decision as to what is to take place should be a matter of government policy and regulation. I might quarrel with government policy, and I certainly do quarrel with government policy so far as aviation matters are concerned, especially the way in which the government has gone back on its announced policy, but I support the idea that government policy is necessary in arriving at basic decisions so far as civil aviation is concerned.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra has referred to the basic government policy that was set up during the war years, and in particular with the passing of the Aeronautics Act in 1944. In fact, a year earlier it was made clear by the former prime minister, Mr. Aeronautics Act
Mackenzie King, that the main air lines in Canada were to be operated by the government-owned Trans-Canada Air Lines. It was indicated that the feeder lines and non-scheduled services would be open to private companies. It was also made clear that all international services connecting Canada with other countries were to be operated by Trans-Canada Air Lines. While that particular part of government policy was not written into the statute, it was laid down clearly in a statement by the Prime Minister and confirmed from time to time.
I feel that that policy has been gone back on so far as services in Canada are concerned, notably in that Canadian Pacific Air Lines has been permitted to develop lines which certainly are not feeder lines. Their air line map today looks like a main-line operation. Another point in that policy, namely with respect to international air services, has been reversed by the government. I refer to the Pacific air services. Not only was it spelled out and stated clearly by the former prime minister that all international air services were to be operated by Trans-Canada Air Lines, but when an agreement was entered into between Australia and New Zealand on the one hand and Canada on the other for transpacific services, one of the terms was that so far as the Canadian part of the operation was concerned it would be carried on by the government-owned Trans-Canada Air Lines. The Minister of Transport will well remember the nuisance I was in the session of 1948.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO POWER OF MINISTER TO MAKE REGULATIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
In the session of 1948 I tried to get out of the minister in every way known to me, by questions on the orders of the day, by raising it on going into supply, by questions on the minister's estimates and so on, whether or not there was anything in the widely circulating rumour that the government was going to turn over the Pacific service to Canadian Pacific Air Lines. The Minister of Transport was most adroit in his answers; they were answers that seemed to imply that there was nothing to the rumour, that I was all wrong. However, I remember that it was only a week or ten days after the session when I picked up a paper and lo and behold the Pacific service had been turned over by the government to Canadian Pacific Air Lines. It is that sort of thing that I

Aeronautics Act
quarrel with. I will stand by my basic contention that the policy respecting civil aviation, because it is a natural monopoly, has to be determined by the government. Nevertheless I feel it is unfortunate that the government should get hold of a good policy, announce it, lay it down clearly, and then for some reason or other-not explained-change it in various respects.
Another item of government policy-and the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra has already referred to this-relates to the announcement by the present Minister of Trade and Commerce in 1944 when he was minister of munitions and supply to the effect that, commencing one year after the end of the war in Europe, all 'transportation companies operating ground services were to be asked to divest themselves of the ownership of air lines. As the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra said, the purpose seemed to be to prevent the Canadian Pacific Railway from developing Canadian Pacific Air Lines into a large private system. The minister of munitions and supply, as he then was, made it clear to us that he had had a bit of a quarrel with the Canadian Pacific people, and that he also felt that mistakes had been made in the building of railways in this country which he did not want to see repeated so far as air lines were concerned. He felt it was unwise to allow a corporation such as the Canadian Pacific Railway to build up a huge air lines system.
This policy was not only announced by the then minister of munitions and supply but was also written into a statute, namely, the Aeronautics Act, chapter 28 of the statutes of 1944-45. We had a bitter debate over the policy. The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, the hon. member for Lake Centre and others of the Conservative party fought it for all they were worth. There was not much support for it even on the Liberal side. I think that the C.C.F. party probably gave more support to it than the Liberals but at any rate the Liberals voted for it and it was passed. It is spelled out in sections 12, 13 and 14 of the act. There was a decision of parliament to back up the announced policy of the government with respect to that phase of civil aviation.
Time went by, the war in Europe came to an end, and a year or so after I began to wonder when this policy was going to go into effect. I have the necessary data here and may refer to it later when we get to the section, but I remember very well asking the Minister of Trade and Commerce about It one day and he told me very blithely that the date in the act had been changed by

order in council. I was horrified at the thought that a statute had been changed by order in council, and I asked the Minister of Trade and Commerce if it had been tabled. He said yes, that I did not know all the orders in council that were tabled and that I had missed that one. I certainly had. I was curious afterwards as to how a statute could be changed by order in council. Therefore I got in touch with the proper officials to try to get hold of the order in council and I soon found out that there was none.
Therefore I asked the Minister of Trade and Commerce very tactfully in a day or two on the orders of the day if he could tell me the number and date of that order in council. His reply was that his officials had informed him there was no order in council, that it had been done by cabinet decision. We had quite a battle over it, if I may shorten the story, because some of us certainly did not think that cabinet decisions were the proper way to legislate. As a matter of fact we could not see how a statute could be changed by an order in council. Later on in the session the present Prime Minister, who was then minister of justice, admitted to me there had been some mistake about the whole matter, and that it was perfectly true that a statute could not be changed by order in council. In other words, the law still stood that surface transportation companies had to divest themselves of the ownership of air lines.
I kept wondering why this was not done, and in 1947 I learned by asking various questions how the government managed to get around the section of the act which they put in there over the bitter opposition of members of the Progressive Conservative party. I found out how they got around the section which was put in there to implement their own policy. They did so by relying on an escape clause in another section which gave the governor in council the power to issue licences to surface transportation companies in exceptional cases. I well remember the time when the Minister of Trade and Commerce told me that there was a block of 53 licences that had to be cancelled under the terms of section 14 of the act, which implemented the policy about which I am talking. All 53 were reissued under the escape or emergency clause in the act. Believe it or not, every case was an exceptional case.
That makes a farce of statute law, Mr. Chairman. It makes a farce of parliament to force it to put in the act a section which the official opposition did not want. I was in favour of it but a section of the opposition did

Aeronautics Act
not want it. A year or so later the government changed its mind mainly because the Minister of Trade and Commerce got on more friendly terms with the Canadian Pacific, and they just decided they were not going to obey the law as it was passed by parliament. We stand up from time to time and ask for certain changes or improvements in various matters and we are told time and time again that these things cannot be changed because they are statutory. We are told the voice of parliament has decided.
Let us understand what is happening. Parliament has reached the point where it decides, through the weight of the government majority, merely what the government wants to put on the statutes, and if the next day the government does not want to go ahead with what it has decided it gets around it in one way or another. When we reach that section of the act we will see that certain sections are now being repealed.

I wanted to make it clear that there are a number of ways in which government policy has been changed from time to time that I dislike intensely. I dislike it particularly when a clear-cut policy has been laid down that appears to be the policy for all time, and then is changed for reasons that are not made clear to us at all..
Even so I cannot agree with the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra in his suggestion that the air transport board should be an independent judicial body. I feel that matters relating to civil aviation are of such importance that they should be subject to government policy. After all, this is a field in which a great deal is at stake. Aviation does not only play an important part in the development of our country in transportation, communications and so on; it is also a field in which the protection of life and safety measures are of extreme importance. I am satisfied it is not a field in which there should be the kind of unrestricted competition that some of our friends to the right would like to have. When you go in for that sort of thing you decrease the safety factor as competing lines try to get ahead of one another.
