subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO POWER OF MINISTER TO MAKE REGULATIONS, ETC.
speechtext: The circular reads:

Circular No. 15
Operation of commercial air services to and from
Canada by foreign air carriers other than agreed services on specified routes by designated air lines
The information to be furnished and the procedure to be followed by foreign air carriers who wish to operate commercial air services, to or from Canada, other than agreed air services operated on specified routes by designated air lines, is laid down in air transport board circular No. 14, which became effective May 15, 1949. This supplements the said circular and outlines the policy which is followed by the air transport board in dealing with applications for permit to operate commercial air services to and from Canada.
When the proposed movement is between Canada and a country with which Canada has a bilateral air agreement providing for agreed air services between the two countries-
(a)	The board believes that the appropriate designated air carriers of the two countries have primary rights to the carriage of traffic between those two countries and requires to be satisfied that one or other of such designated air carriers is not in a position to furnish the proposed transportation on a reasonable basis;
(b)	If the appropriate designated air carrier of one or other of the countries is not in a position to furnish the proposed transportation, the board prefers that the traffic be carried by some other air carrier of one of the two countries;
(c)	If the board is satisfied that one air carrier of one country or the other is unable to furnish the transportation on a reasonable basis; and if the board is satisfied that the transportation applied for would be in the public interest, then it is prepared to grant a permit to the air carrier of a third country;
(d)	Any large movement involving frequency, regularity or volume, is reviewed with care. When the applicant is a carrier of a third country, the board would refuse a permit unless satisfied that the traffic should be moved by air carrier of a third country and in such cases may require either association with an appropriate designated air line if any, or some other form of direct governmental sponsorship from one of the two countries involved;
(e)	In dealing with applications from foreign air carriers under the foregoing principles, the board takes into consideration primarily the position of the Canadian air carriers, assuming that the other country from, or to which the proposed movement is to take place, will protect the interests of its own carriers.
(f)	In all such cases the board reviews the proposed charges and conditions of carriage to make sure that they are just and reasonable.
When the proposed movement is between Canada and a country with which Canada has no bilateral agreement-
(a)	The board requires to be satisfied that it is in the public interest that the transportation be furnished by an air carrier other than the designated air carriers whose combined services connect Canada and that country.
(b)	If the board is so satisfied, preference would normally be given to carriage by either a Canadian carrier or a carrier of the country to or from which the traffic is moving. A reasonable liberal attitude is taken towards applications from the carriers of third countries for occasional flights. In the case of large or frequent movements however, the board
Aeronautics Act
takes the general attitude indicated in 2(d) above.
(c)	A rate review on the basis indicated in 2(f) above also takes place.
Air Transport Board
Gerald Morisset,
Secretary.
Ottawa, Ontario,
August 31, 1949.
Section agreed to.
On section 3-Powers of minister to make regulations with approval of governor in council.

The explanatory note dealing with new clause (d) reads:
This amendment is intended: To mark clearly the application of the paragraph to the use and operation of aircraft as distinguished from the economic regulation of commercial air services.
That raises a question as to where the boundary is between the work done by the minister and his aviation branch and the work of the air transport board; because the air transport board deals with economic regulation of all commercial air services. A few minutes ago, when I asked the minister to explain just where the boundary was, he said he would wait until he got to a section of the bill; and I think this is the section on which that answer should be given.

A while ago the hon. member made the point that the air transport board did not possess sufficient power and authority, that it should have more power and authority, and that it should not be subject to the approval of the minister with regard to the granting of licences; and he argued in favour of a completely independent board, as did his leader the other evening, I think.
That is dealing with the judicial functions.

Yes. There is a reason why that situation should be as it is, because the air transport board has to deal with a problem which is entirely different from that where there would be nothing but independent air carriers, as in the United States, for instance. In Canada the largest operator is a government-owned air line, and I think it would be improper for the board to have exclusive powers such as my hon. friend argues for with reference to a government-owned body such as T.C.A. In other words it is felt that the board should have powers to advise on routes concerning T.C.A., and powers to advise economically as it does, but tha't there should be a limitation, as is set out in the amendment, because of this special position in respect of T.C.A.
My hon. friend asks for a division of the powers as between the departmental officials

Aeronautics Act
and air transport board officials or as between the minister and the board. They are fairly clearly set out in part I as opposed to part II. In committee the other day I think I gave at some length the functions of the air transport board and the duties of the air transport board under the various sections. This section seeks to change the words:
The conditions under which aircraft may be used for carrying goods, mails and passengers, or for the operation of any commercial service whatsoever;
To:	.
The conditions under which aircraft may be used or operated; . . .
So that there will be a distinction between the powers of the department or the powers of the minister and those of the board. In the language used before, among the departmental officials there was some feeling that there was an impingement of the duties of the board, and the amendment is sought to clarify the duties as between the board and the department.

When I was speaking on
section 1, I mentioned the government policy which restricts competition on these different routes. That apparently is underlying government policy not set out in any statute, order in council or directive but which, according to the chairman of the air transport board, is obviously considered by him to be binding upon the board. Can the minister give us any clarification of that particular policy and tell us whether or not there is any other policy of some kind which is not written into the statutes or not in an order in council but which, nevertheless, is recognized as government policy in the field of civil aviation?

In the committee the policy was gone into at some length. It is somewhat technical, and I do not know that I should like to give it again. It can be found in the evidence. But the board follows the government policy. That policy has been announced in the house here on more than one occasion.
You are referring to the policy announced in 1944, are you?
I think it was 1943.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

speechtext:
In 1943, dealing with domestic scheduled routes, and that not more than one carrier should operate on any one route. I think my predecessor did announce that at that time. The board follow that policy, of course. But more than that, the board are in agreement on that policy and believe that it is correct. Otherwise the board could, under its advisory powers, make recommendations to the contrary to the minister

who would take it up with his colleagues in the cabinet in order to ascertain whether the policy should remain as it is or be amended.

Then on page 3, clause 6, we
find this provision:
Any regulation made under subsection one may authorize the minister to make orders or directions with respect to such matters coming within this section as the regulations may prescribe.
The explanatory note at the side is as follows:
Minister may carry out regulations by ministerial order or direction.
We went into that at length in committee, and I think it will be agreed that what is sought here is power for the minister to issue directives which will have the same force and effect as if they were regulations and, of course, would carry the same penalty.
Hon. members will find at page 3 of the bill a new provision for penalties, where it is indicated that the penalty may be $5,000 or imprisonment for a term not exceeding one year, or to both fine and imprisonment. That punishment is to apply to the directives issued by the minister, just as it applies to the regulations passed by the governor in council. I do not think that is giving the person who may be fined or put in jail a fair run for his money. I say that for these reasons:
Under part III of the Aeronautics Act all regulations have to be published in the Canada Gazette; furthermore they must be laid before the House of Commons within ten days after publication, if parliament is then sitting or, if parliament is not sitting, within ten days after the commencement of the next ensuing session thereof. This means that parliament took care to give the public a chance to know what the regulations are. That is as it should be, because it is a serious thing to put a man in jail for a year.
If the minister has to issue directives covering certain conditions which may arise, then there should be some different sort of punishment for breach of those directives, rather than making the culprit subject to fine up to $5,000, or to imprisonment for a year, or both fine and imprisonment. The minister is given wide powers to cancel or suspend licences. If these directives are issued and then are not followed, I believe it would be sufficient punishment to suspend a licence for a time, or even to cancel it. But, instead of that, a breach of these directives is made just as serious as a breach of the regulations; yet there is no provision for publicizing directives, and there is no way in which it can be made certain that the people in this business will know what directives have been issued.

For that reason I would urge that the minister make provision in the act whereby punishment for a breach of the directives shall not be the same as that for a breach of the regulations.

Is there any difference
between regulations, orders and directives?

If this amendment is passed as it now stands there will be no difference in the punishment for a breach. The section indicates, as explained in the side note, that the minister may carry out regulations by ministerial order or direction. I think the proper procedure would be to issue a new regulation. It does not take long, because regulations could be passed by the cabinet within a matter of a few days. But this amendment goes further than that. He may issue a directive, then the day after this amendment is passed if that directive is not complied with the person guilty of the offence can be dragged into court and fined or imprisoned.

If that is so, it seems to me that the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra has raised an important point. I am not a lawyer and not given to interpreting some of these legal phrases; but I am just wondering about a provision whereby the minister is authorized to make orders and directions with respect to such matters as come within this section, as the regulations may provide, and then the further provision which states that: Every person who violates the provisions of a regulation is guilty of an offence and is liable on summary conviction to a fine not exceeding five thousand dollars, or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding one year or to both fine and imprisonment.
If the interpretation placed upon the section by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra is correct, whereby the minister may issue a directive or order which would not be confirmed by an order in council, as a regulation would be, and to which no publicity is given, then it seems to me the hon. member is right in his criticism of this proposal. Would the minister given an explanation of it?

If I may be permitted to make an observation on the same point, I suppose the minister and his officials have perhaps surrendered to one of the inevitable trends of human nature, that of trying to find an easier administrative way to handle the situation quickly, even though it may be at the expense of the public generally.
This situation takes us along the road of order-in-council government just another mile, it seems to me-only it takes us along the road not only in daylight, but another mile in the dark. I say that because if this amendment is accepted the minister may, if 55946-180
Aeronautics Act
he wishes, prosecute someone who has not even learned that he is violating the law, and has no way of finding out what law he is violating.
No, that is not so.
As I read the section it is so.
No.

Unless one happens to be in the cabinet, one will not know what the law is-and there are not many in the cabinet, even though there are a number on the opposite side of the chamber who would like to find themselves there.
Would the hon. member be a little more serious.

I am sorry that this section is not a little more serious, because the position the minister has taken today reflects a mentality, so far as the government is concerned, that is anything but serious when dealing with the ordinary public.
Oh no.

I suggest that before this section is carried the committee should be told just where we are going. Not only are we travelling in the dark; we are going in the opposite direction to that which I think the public wants us to follow. The public does not want us to place more authority in the hands of the executive, but rather to bring the procedure of law-making back into the parliamentary system whereby the representatives of the people shall have some control over the laws the people must obey.
The minister should further consider whether in the final analysis he requires anything like this amount of power. This is adding more fads and frills to order-incouncil government that the public would not like to have-and I do not like it, either.

I was going to say that perhaps if we were to get back to a somewhat calmer discussion of the section we would make greater headway. The questions asked were normal ones, and I should like to answer them to the satisfaction of the committee. I believe the committee is entitled to know just what the section means and how it will work, and I shall try to give that information.
Section 4 of the present act says that with the approval of the governor in council the minister may make orders and regulations with respect to licensing pilots, registration and identification of aircraft, stating conditions under which aircraft can be used for carrying goods, the conditions under which goods may be exported or imported, and the

Aeronautics Act
like. The moment those orders in council are passed they are gazetted and are open tor public inspection.
This section goes a step further, I must admit, and provides:
Any regulation made under subsection one may authorize the minister to make orders or directions with respect to such matters coming within this section as the regulations may prescribe.
The officials of the department think that that is necessary. I think the committee should know that there are times when because of emergency or urgency it is impossible to move quickly enough by means of an order in council. I could give some examples. An accident occurred to a Moth aircraft in which a passenger was killed and a pilot injured, as the result of the aircraft getting into a spin at low altitude because of jammed controls. The operators and pilots of this type of aircraft were cautioned to see, first, that the passenger's safety belt is fastened; second, that the control column and rudder connections are removed; and, third, that the control box cover is fastened in place. The circular is sent out making it mandatory that these things be done for the protection of the passenger flying in that type of aircraft. That is not done by order in council because it would take too long.
How long would it take?

Anywhere from four days to two weeks or even longer depending upon the amount of work the government had at the time. There are a number of other examples I could give which might be more important than this one. There are thousands of circumstances in which it is important to issue orders and directives. If it were necessary to ask the minister to get an order in council and submit it to cabinet it would take a considerable amount of time.
Here is one having to do with the condition of the airstrips at Gander. During a certain period of the year when the frost comes out of the ground planes weighing above a certain tonnage may not land on the airstrips. The frost comes out of the ground quite suddenly and if it were necessary to get an order in council through before the directive or circular was issued, it would take too long. It is necessary that this be done by a directive or order.
Here is another case where it is provided that no person in an aircraft shall carry out acrobatic flying over any city or town or populous district. Second, shall not carry out any acrobatic flying or exhibition flying over any regatta, race meeting or meeting for public games or sports except when specially arranged for in writing by the promoters of

such regatta or meeting and authorized by the minister. Third, shall not carry out any flying which, by reason of low altitude or proximity to persons or dwellings, is dangerous to public safety.
Many accidents have taken place because of a breach of this order. This order has not the force of law; it has only the force of a circular.

It seems to me that in the cases cited, particularly this last one, it would be quite simple to have a regulation. I am not so sure about the one dealing with the frost at Gander or perhaps the danger disclosed in connection with flying in Moth aircraft, but in a case of wide application I cannot see the force of having an order rather than a regulation.

That may be so, but I am told that these orders and directives that are put out in circular form run into the hundreds. I have quite a number of them here and could go on and on. While the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra took exception in the committee the other day to this amendment, I think the feeling generally was that these orders and regulations were of such importance that they should be given the effect of law. It is not something new. If the committee is surprised at what appears to be the granting of powers that are said to be out of the ordinary, let me say that this is done under the Customs Act as well as under the Animal Contagious Diseases Act. It is done in the United Kingdom where they have had far more experience than we. I can assure the committee that it is not a question of taking powers that seem to be irregular and out of the ordinary.
If it were possible to pass an order in council to cover each case, I think it should be done. But it cannot be done as it would be too cumbersome. For that reason the officers of the department have suggested that we should follow what has been done in the Customs Act and the Animal Contagious Diseases Act and give the force of law to orders and directives. There is no secrecy about these orders and regulations, and I hope the committee has not got that impression. They are circulated to all fliers and to all owners and operators of air lines because we want to give them as much publicity as possible. It is important that publicity be given to them; that they should not be kept hidden.
Does the minister sign these directives himself?
As it is now, I do not sign them; they are sent out as circulars. If this amendment passes, yes, I would sign them.
There will be none put out except as signed by the minister?
The minister or the deputy minister.
The minister. He is the one who takes the responsibility.
Yes, they would be signed by the minister.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Do I understand that so far these orders and directives do not have the force of law?
That is right, and they do not have to be obeyed.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The department and the minister feel that they should be made obligatory by order in council?
That is right.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I notice it is suggested that the penalty for infractions of these regulations be increased from $1,000 to $5,000. Is that because there has been too much disregard of some of these orders and regulations?

There are two reasons for increasing the penalty. First, it was thought that the penalties for infractions of sections under part I of the act should be the same as the penalties for infractions under part II. Another reason is that there have been some infractions, although I cannot say that they have been numerous, and it was thought desirable to have a higher penalty.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Has the minister any information as to the number of infractions and what class of operator has been most guilty?
I have not that at hand, but I can get it.

I suggest that this is moving in a very dangerous direction. The minister has said that there are hundreds of directives. If they are to be issued in this easy way then several results will follow. One will be that practically everything will be done by directive. There will be no incentive to have regulations. It is so much easier simply to draw up an order and have the minister or deputy minister sign it, and that will be the normal course followed. I suggest it will mean a good many more directives than there would be if some restriction were placed on the power to issue orders of this kind.
Surely there should not be the same penalty for breach of a directive as there is for breach of a regulation. For example, if the section is passed in its present form, a person can be given the same punishment for breaking one of these ministerial directives as
55946-180i
Aeronautics Act
he would receive for operating a forty-passenger plane without a commercial licence. The penalty is exactly the same. In the standing committee we asked general counsel for the department whether or not it was the intention that there should be prosecutions under these directives. At page 262 of the proceedings of the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, he said:
I think that would have to depend on the regulations themselves. And if the regulation said that certain directives of the minister had to be complied with, then I would think that non-compliance with the directives would involve a breach of the regulations which would result in a possible prosecution. It might come back to the regulations themselves and be treated as a breach of regulations.
That would have to be decided by the court, and would the court not take into consideration how serious the breach was?
Just as in any other summary procedure.

If parliament passes this
section it will be making a breach of the directives as serious a matter as a breach of the regulations, and crown counsel will be within his rights to argue that before the judge. I suggest that the penalty for a breach of these directives should be different from the penalty for a breach of the regulations. For example, the minister already has power under the act to suspend a licence. If he finds any flier or firm committing a breach of the terms of a directive then he can meet that situation by suspending the licence. In fact that would probably be just as effective as if court action were taken. It is going very far for parliament to say that it will give the minister the authority to issue an order, a breach of which carries exactly the same penalty as a breach of the regulations which must be approved not by one minister or one deputy minister but by cabinet. Regulations have the judgment of other members of the cabinet, are then duly published, and people all over the country have some chance to know that there is such a regulation in force.
I do not think there can be any justification for putting a ministerial directive on the same basis as a regulation passed by order in council. If the amendment is passed in its present form that is exactly what parliament is doing.

The hon. member suggests that perhaps we would be better off by suspending the licence. I think we would be far worse off if we were to suspend the licence. We have given this matter very careful consideration. I can imagine what would happen if, because of a breach of these orders, the licence was suspended.

Aeronautics Act
Immediately there would be a great cry, "We did not get a chance to defend ourselves before the licence was taken from us". When there are automobile accidents on highways drivers' licences are not suspended without other things being done first. First of all a charge of criminal negligence, speeding or something else, is laid in a police court. If the magistrate so wishes he may, over and above fining the individual or imposing a prison term, suspend his licence. We can also do that, but I think it would be a mistake to suspend the licence without other action being first taken. It would be going much further than we would sometimes wish to go.
The other point raised was as to placing a directive, so far as fine or imprisonment is concerned, on the same basis as a regulation. The fact is that some of the orders and directives made under order in council are far more important, and the breach thereof is far more serious, than some of the regulations made under order in council. That is the reason why it has been found necessary to do this, and it seems to me. that it is the proper thing to do under the circumstances.

Mr. Chairman, I listened to the minister with some interest when he said that the same provision was in the Animal Contagious Diseases Act and in the Customs Act. Would he mention the sections of the Animal Contagious Diseases Act and the Customs Act to which he made reference, and would he also read in full the sections to which he refers?

I do not have them before
me but I am informed, so that there will be no doubt about my sincerity of purpose-
I know that.

I am informed by the
Department of Justice that similar provisions are contained in the Animal Contagious Diseases Act and other statutes whereby orders and directives are made under authorized regulations. I cannot point to the section but if I got the act I presume I could. I am informed on good authority that such is the case.
The minister says that it takes from four days to two weeks to pass an order in council. I think that is rather longer than it takes.
Mr. Chairman, I do not think the hon. member wants to put words in my mouth.

If I said that, perhaps I did not use the correct language. It does not take from four days to two weeks to pass an order in council. It takes a very short time to pass an order in council, but it takes from four days to two weeks before an order in council can be considered. It has to be prepared, it has to be brought before the subcommittee of cabinet dealing with it. There might not be time at the particular meeting dealing with orders in council to consider all of them, and it is held over for another meeting.
What is the average number dealt with per day?
It is not a question of per day; it is a question of per meeting. It might be 5,000. I am advised on some occasions there have been as many as 5,000.

Mr. Chairman, this is even worse than I thought it was. Certainly it shows the extent to which orders in council, including of course treasury orders, are passed. I have been trying to help the minister.
May I say that my reference was to 5,000 a year.

Of course it is a great many more than 5,000 a year. As a matter of fact it must run to five times 5,000 at the very least. I have not the latest figures but I am very much interested in the rather easy manner in which the minister brushes aside all objections raised by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra. He gave certain examples where haste was necessary. One example was low flying. Surely that must be an offence now under the regulations. That example did not appeal as a basis for having laws made by officials of the department. This looks like a short cut suggested by officials in order to get things done without having laws made, either by order in council or through parliament.
To say that the penalty is the same in a directive as in a regulation constitutes a serious derogation of legislative authority. It means that two or three officials of the department can simply make out such a directive as appeals to them at the moment, hand it to the minister and say, "We need action on this immediately." This is not going to apply retroactively; therefore I see no reason for this haste. This is not done in the United Kingdom. Only the other day I was reading a debate that took place in the House of Lords, and this is one thing that is simply not done. Within the last ten days, speaking in the House of Lords, Viscount Cecil of Chelwood used these words:
The growing power of the cabinet is a danger to the democratic constitution of the country.

He was referring to the power of the cabinet to issue orders in council. This amendment places authority over the liberty of the subject in the hands of officials, who may decide that they are in a rush for action and issue a directive to meet their own desires thus penalizing the individual. Viscount Simon dealt with the matter also, and used these words:
The rule of law has largely ceased to protect citizens of this country over a wide range of rights and liabilities.
That is just what these orders and directives would do. This amendment will give an official in this department power to say to one person, "I issue a directive making it an offence in your case punishable by a heavy fine, whereas it does not apply to another person." This denies the rule of law and equality as between individuals, and I am surprised that the minister presses this amendment so assiduously. After all, he has tremendous powers under section 4, providing for almost every eventuality, certainly everything contemplated by the minister at the time the act was passed. There would be no abnegation of authority if the minister were to withdraw this amendment. When I first heard my hon. friend and colleague dealing with the matter I could not conceive that the minister had gone so far. Surely this power is not needed. He mentioned as an example the frost going out in Gander airport. Well, I would imagine the frost goes out there at about the same time each year. That may be an unusual case, but surely one unusual case does not justify parliament absolutely abdicating its legislative authority and putting in the hands of one official power over the liberty of the subject. This.is a request on the part of the minister to put officialdom in a position where, if they see something wrong, even if it is but a peccadillo, they may decide to issue a directive and impose punishment by means of a fine not exceeding $5,000 or one year in jail.
Punishment like that should not be within the discretion of an official in the department. Coming back to my main objection, apart from those raised by my hon. friend, this places the minister or his officials in a position where they can discriminate, where they can continue to deny the application of the rule of law, where they can pass laws to meet peculiar situations and make individuals liable to the penalties set out. I suggest to the minister that, in the interests of the preservation of the rights of the individual against unjust or tyrannical directives, this amendment should be withdrawn.
Aeronautics Act
As a matter of fact it is interesting to note that in the explanations the reason for asking for this amendment is this:
To provide for proper enforcement of detailed safety procedures requiring frequent change . . .
In other words we may have one law today and another tomorrow, not based upon the considered judgment of the minister but upon the caprice of the moment. Tremendous improvements have been made within the last two years in this country in connection with order in council government. The Prime Minister has gone so far as to have orders in council regularly tabled, and legislation now before parliament will increase the opportunity of the individual to ascertain what is the law. Having this in mind, this section is actually a retrograde step. Such authority should not be in the hands of officials who at a given moment may be antagonized by the attitude of one person and who, without intending to do so, still have power to discriminate.
Knowing the minister as I do I feel sure that on reconsideration he will withdraw this amendment. He has very wide powers already under section 4. This amendment will simply give him and his officials carte blanche to do as they please in individual cases, regardless of what may be the application of the law in general cases.

If the hon. member for Lake Centre is right of course this amendment would be wholly bad. But is it true to say that a directive may be issued discriminating against one individual, more or less at the caprice of some official? Is it not a fact, or am I wrong, that an order or directive so issued would have general application, and not application to only a particular individual at a particular time?
If I may answer that question now, it would have general application. It would be issued as a circular to the pilot, the owner and the operator.

A little earlier the matter of low flying was mentioned, and no doubt other orders and directives of a similar nature have been issued. I can see that it might happen that such orders or directives must be issued within a few hours, if there is an emergency; but when that happens should they not be subsequently issued as regulations, with the authority of an order in council, if as the minister says they are sufficiently important that they should have general application? It seems to me that while there may be occasions when something unforeseen may happen and it is necessary to issue an immediate order or directive, that immediate order or directive issued

Aeronautics Act
because of the necessity of the moment should, if it is to have general application thereafter, be the subject of a regulation issued in the usual way by order in council and published. As I said earlier when I first drew attention to this, to my mind the section is worded in such a way that it is difficult to understand just what the implication is, because it speaks of the violation of the provisions of a regulation, not an order or directive. There is confusion, I believe, in the manner in which it is worded.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member suggests that in important instances, such as those that were mentioned earlier in the discussion, the orders and directives should be tabled or made the subject of a regulation at a later date. I can see some merit in that, and I would not have any objection, if it were the wish of the committee, that all orders and directives be tabled so that the house would know what was in them.

That was not my only point. If they are of general interest, then it seems to me they should cease to be mere orders and directives, and should become regulations in the same sense as other regulations, with the authority of the government through order in council. That is the point I am making; not necessarily tabling them but converting them, if they are of general importance, into proper regulations with the authority of order in council.

Apparently the minister is not going to do anything about changing this section, and that means the responsibility rests with him. As has been pointed out by other speakers, this section is not drafted properly. I think there are different ways in which it could be corrected, but the minister has not yet-
How does the hon. member suggest it should be remedied?
The member for Rosetown-Biggar made one suggestion.
He suggested it should be withdrawn.

The member for Rosetown-Biggar made one suggestion, that if there were need for regulations to be passed on short notice or for some action to be taken quickly, then a directive should be issued, and the directive should be made a regulation within a set period. Such a procedure would eliminate my main objection. There are different ways in which the evil in this proposed amendment could be dealt with. Another way would be to provide for a penalty which is not so severe.

In view of the fact the minister is not accepting any of these suggestions, and apparently wants to push this section through in its present form, I move, Mr. Chairman, that clause 6 of section 3 of the bill be deleted.
Mr. Chairman, for the reasons I gave earlier, and because of the discussion which took place in committee on this matter at some length, I would have to oppose the amendment of the member.
Would the minister reconsider the whole situation in the light of what has been said this afternoon, and perhaps allow the section to stand?

No, I am not prepared to reconsider it because I was asked to do that when the bill was before the committee on railways, canals, and telegraph lines. I gave the matter careful consideration, and came back and gave the reasons why I thought it was necessary that orders and directives be made.

Apparently the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra agrees with the suggestion I made, that if orders or directives have general application and are of sufficient importance, then they should be made regulations by order in council. It seems to me that if the minister agrees to that he removes the objection the member for Vancouver-Quadra has, and that I feel has some validity. I do not want, Mr. Chairman, to deny the minister the right, in an emergency, to issue an order or directive temporarily, so long as it is regularized afterwards, if it is of general application.

I did not deal with that point for the reason that, if that were consented to, then it would defeat the purpose of the amendment entirely. Who is going to decide how important these directives are? The hon. member may feel they were all important, and that being so orders in council by way of regulation would have to be passed to cover them all.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
One order in council could cover fifty directives. There is one point about the wording of these sections about which I am still not clear. I wish the minister would follow what I am trying to say, and I should also like the member for Lake Centre to follow it, to see if we can get this thing sorted out.
Subsection 2, starting at line 5 on page 3, says:
Any regulation made under subsection one may authorize the minister to make orders or directions . . .

Now, subsection 1 gives the governor in council the power to make regulations respecting air navigation. Subsection 3, starting at line 11 on page 3, says:
Every person who violates the provisions of a regulation is guilty of an offence . . .
Supposing a regulation is passed by order in council giving the minister power to make certain directives. If I violate that regulation, it is clear I am guilty of an offence, but when the minister, under that regulation, isues an order or directive and I violate that order or directive, have I violated the regulation?

I suppose that is a question of law, but certainly the order would have been violated. It is the object of this amendment to penalize, by way of a fine or imprisonment, a person who has violated an order made under the regulation.

These regulations are for the protection of life and property. Since I have lived beside a large airport for a good many years, it occurs to me that these regulations cannot be too strict. Quick decisions must be made, and authority must be given to the men at these airports to act quickly. Many accidents are caused by people who wilfully disobey regulations with respect to landing at airports on the northwest staging route. Our friends from the United States are sinners in that regard. They come in their private planes, and very often neglect to obey simple regulations which are set down for the protection of life. Without going into a legal quibble about language, it would seem to me that the stronger these regulations are made, and the more authority you give for the protection of human life, the better it will be for everyone concerned.
This is not a matter of riding a bicycle on the street, or something of that sort. When a passenger plane, possibly carrying fifty passengers, comes in for a landing, and there are some small craft flying about, and not obeying the regulations, somebody has got to act quickly. The penalty should be increased rather than decreased.

We are not discussing the regulations, Mr. Chairman. This is a matter of an order or directive issued under a regulation. I hesitate to deny to the minister the power that is asked for, because I can see that in the interests of safety and so on it may be necessary to issue an order. I can see that immediately. But once an order is issued which has a general application and is found to be essential to the safety of the travelling public, I am wondering if that
Aeronautics Act
should not be regularized by order in council and made a regulation instead of an order or directive. That is the point that I have in mind, and just that one point. I do not feel that I would be justified in denying the power that is asked for, but I would like the safeguard.

Once again, Mr. Chairman,
in answer to that I cannot say any more than I have already said.
I think the minister understands what I mean.

I fully understand, and I appreciate the point. I think that is the only point that has been made in the discussion, and it has been made by more than one member; that is the point as to the section making the same penalty applicable to violators of the order or directive as is applicable to violators of the regulation. It may well be that there should be a difference between the penalties in those two cases. After having listened to the points that were made, I think perhaps there is something in the argument. But I think it would be a mistake to wipe out the whole clause. My hon. friend shakes his head. I know that he is not asking for that and neither did the leader of the Social Credit party ask for that; but that has been asked for-
I said if you are willing to amend it that will be perfectly all right.

Let me go on. After listening to the discussion I think perhaps there is a reason for differentiating between violation of a regulation and violation of a directive or order, by way of a variation in the punishment and penalty; and I would be prepared to accept an amendment. In fact, I am prepared to move one which would leave the penalty for the infraction of the order or regulation as it is now, and is as follows:
Amend subclause (7) of clause 3 of Bill 153 by adding the following as subsection (4):
4. Every person who violates an order or direction of the minister made under a regulation is guilty of an offence and is liable on summary conviction to a fine not exceeding one thousand dollars or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding six months or to both fine and imprisonment.
I would ask my colleague to make this motion accordingly.
I move accordingly.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Is it the pleasure of the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra to withdraw his own amendment, in view of the amendment suggested by the minister?

Even at that, I am much against this business of issuing directives. I would,

Aeronautics Act
however, be willing to withdraw my amendment, provided that this amendment to the next clause is put forward by the government.
Oh, yes. The Minister of National Defence moves accordingly.

Agreed.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The house in committee on Bill No. 153.

On a matter of privilege, I did not check very closely the Hansard report of my speech yesterday, and at page 2808, in the 16th line, it reads, "As I listened to him over the air." It should read, "As I listened to the report over the air."
I, along with others, did hear this news report over a Winnipeg station the morning of May 18, attributing to the mayor of Winnipeg the statement charging the premier of Manitoba with criminal neglect.
Also in this afternoon's Ottawa Journal is the report of a denial by Mayor Garnet Coulter. I should like to read it:
Mayor Garnet Coulter last night denied "very firmly that he had ever accused Premier Douglas Campbell of maladministration in the Manitoba flood crisis.
He was replying to a statement made in the House of Commons by J. A. Ross (P.C.-Souris). Mr. Ross said he had heard the Winnipeg mayor charge in a radio broadcast that the premier had been "guilty of criminal negligence" in his handling of the situation.
"In one of the meetings of the city's flood-control committee," Mayor Coulter said, "there was somewhat harsh criticism of Premier Campbell, but not by me.
"It is possible that some such expression (as that referred to by Mr. Ross) was used."
I checked the Winnipeg Tribune of May 17, and found that the deputy mayor, Alderman C. E. Simonite, is reported on the front page, in heavy type, as having made that statement.

I accept the denial of Mayor Garnet Coulter, and I wish to apologize and make amends to him.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: We were discussing section 6.
What change is there in this section with regard to tolls?

My hon. friend, I understand, is dealing with section 6(g). The only change in section 6(g) is the addition of the word "toll" after the word "tariff." This is a change in phraseology. It was felt that because the word "toll" covered a wider field than "tariff" it should be inserted. It is also felt that a tariff is a document including charges filed with the board, whereas a toll is a specific charge.
I had reference more particularly to the new paragraph (gg).

This change is for the same reason as those in sections 2(4) and 4(1). It is to give to the board jurisdiction over tolls outside the territorial jurisdiction of Canada. I think the note opposite section 2(4) would give an exact explanation of this amendment. As the act stands today there is no jurisdiction to cover tolls outside Canada, and because of commitments made by ICAO it is felt there should be jurisdiction in that respect.

There is a provision being written into section 12 of the act the effect of which would be to give the board power to exempt international routes. If they are exempt from the control of the board, then why does the board retain any jurisdiction over the tolls?

There cannot just be the casual interpretation that the minister places on the subsection. It was put in the act clearly for the purpose of implementing the policy as announced by the government at that time. Although I have not Hansard of that long debate before me at this moment I am sure that when that subsection was being discussed the minister of munitions and supply made it clear that that was in the act for the purpose of implementing that policy. In 1947 I asked the minister how the surface transportation companies were to be permitted to operate air lines beyond a year after the end of the war in Europe, and the Minister of Trade and Commerce told me that that was done by cancelling all the licences of these companies-there were fifty-three-and reissuing them under the terms of section 12, subsection 2.
I contend that that escape clause in subsection 2 is at variance with the purpose of the section in the original act. If the government has changed its policy, if it is no longer the intention of the government to deny to surface transportation companies the right to operate air lines, they should not leave this now meaningless subsection in the statute.

Does not the minister think that having extra restrictions of this kind in the act may prevent transportation companies from entering the field of civil aviation? With that restriction in the act a company operating busses or a shipping company might not even consider establishing an air line. I am wondering whether it would not be wise to take the subsection out of the act unless it is government policy that there shall be extra restrictions in effect against any company in the transportation business.
If that is the policy of the government then I can see the value of this subsection, but the actions of the last two or three years would indicate that that is no longer the policy. Such being the case it does seem unwise to have a restrictive provision of this kind which certainly is not an inducement to transportation companies to enter the air business.

My hon. friend asks if I do not think it is a deterrent. I do not think it is, any more than it was in the case of the subsidiaries of the railway companies, the T.C.A. and the C.P.A. -unless the governor in council is of opinion that it is in the public interest that such licence be issued.
