The house in committee of supply, Mr. Beaudoin in the chair.

Mr. Chairman, I wonder if the committee would consent to my calling item No. 523, because it has to do with the air transport .board. We have been discussing

Supply-Transport
it, no matter what their age may be. Actually it is very difficult for men who have followed the sea to obtain other work, particularly if they are forty years of age, or so. To give them vocational training would be a great help.
Then, another way in which the restrictions are too severe is that an applicant apparently must have signed a contract with a manning pool. I am told that in many cases young men were not allowed to sign manning pool contracts. If a young lad of seventeen or eighteen went into the merchant navy they would not sign him, because of his age. Yet now he finds that he cannot qualify for training because he did not sign a manning pool contract. Under the present regulations also he must prove that he was eligible for the special bonus which was paid to the men of the merchant navy. In some cases men served on Canadian ships who were not signed up under contract or who for one reason or another did not get that bonus and so cannot qualify for the training. I do not understand why the department is so strict in laying down the rules. It would seem to me that if a man served on a Canadian ship and was honourably discharged he should be eligible for vocational training, particularly in view of the fact that he gets practically no other benefits.
There is another reason why something should be done. Within the last few months there has been a drastic reduction in the number of available jobs on Canadian ships as a result of the policy of transferring ships to British registry. Many hundreds of men were put out of work. In announcing the new shipping policy toward the end of the last session the Prime Minister said that the provisions for training would be extended in order to help men who were bound to lose their jobs when the Canadian ships were transferred. Yet the extension under the regulations has not been sufficient to meet these cases and I urge upon the minister that such step be taken now; that we throw open vocational training to any men who served on Canadian ships during the war.
This is having a direct effect, not only upon the present but upon the future Canadian merchant marine. We have always been a maritime people but we cannot hope to have a merchant marine if we do not treat these men properly. There are men in all the seaports of Canada who have had experience on Canadian ships and who feel they have not received a fair deal. In my opinion they are quite right; I think they have had shabby treatment. It may be because there are so few of them, it may be because they are to be found largely in the seaports, or it may be because of the attitude taken by officials of the
[Mr. Green.1
Department of Transport. I sometimes won der whether they are not working under th old principle that the only way to get alon; with a sailor is to kick him around.
In my opinion this failure to give thesi merchant seamen adequate vocational traininj and other benefits is going to have a seriou effect on Canadian shipping in the future There is much talk these days of more trouble of another war. If by any sad chance then should be more fighting a Canadian merchan navy will be needed just as much as, ant perhaps more than, it was in the last war. Wi are not laying a very good foundation for < Canadian merchant navy by this niggardl; treatment of men who served in the merchan navy during the last war.

Can the minister give us : little more information on this subject of voca tional training? The vote is decreased fron $350,000 last year to $50,000 this year, and should like to know the reason. Can he tel us where the training is given, the number o: applicants who were trained and the numbe: rejected?

I put most of that informa tion on Hansard the other evening. I gavi the reason for the decrease by stating tha there was to be a supplementary estimate ii the neighbourhood of $150,000. I placed oi Hansard answers to the questions which m; hon. friend has asked.
At what centres is thi: training given?

The two orders in council an administered jointly by the Department o: Transport and the Department of Veteran: Affairs. The application is made to the Department of Transport and the administratior is under the Department of Veterans Affairs My understanding is that the vocational training is given in various schools across Canada but I am afraid I cannot state just where thej are located.
Can the minister give anj information with regard to the entrance requirements for this training?
It is set out in the orders ir council. A person is entitled to vocationa! training who signed a manning pool agreemen' or who received a war risk or special bonus
I am told by a numbe: of merchant seamen in Toronto that the centre there is the Ryerson Institute anc that the entrance requirements are such tha few merchant seamen can qualify for th< courses.

It is not a question of ability to take the course, it is a question of i

In the report of the Department of Trans-iort for the year ended March 31, 1949, we ind the whole subject matter dealt with inder the heading, "Rehabilitation of Mer-hant Seamen"; when the estimates of he Department of Veterans Affairs are up
cannot proceed because I am told, "We iave nothing to do with this; you will have to ;o to the Department of Transport." I lelieve I am in the right spot now, because he minister in charge is before the com-nittee.
The Depuiy Chairman: I thank the hon. nember for his explanation; but I am won-lering if that does not become a matter of ;overnment policy which might better have ieen discussed under the first item for lepartmental administration.
I assure the hon. member it is difficult to Iraw the line, because there are many sub-ects hon. members may wish to bring in. 5ut according to the standing order, speeches n committee of supply must be strictly rele-rant to the item. If I permit the hon. mem-ler for Vancouver-Quadra to go beyond what s permitted under the item, then I shall iave to give the same freedom to other hon. nembers.
I remember that when the items were icfore the committee of supply on the last ccasion there was a general discussion with espect to merchant seamen, having particu-ar reference to the special headings set out n the details of item 467. I remember that he hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra spoke in that occasion, as did also the hon. member or Cape Breton South. But they did not go ny further than would have been covered iy the subheadings of vocational training and irar medals.
Tonight we did that again, quite properly. 5ut the minute the hon. member refers to heir qualifications for pensions, I am afraid Le is out of order because it would be com->letely extraneous to the subject matter iefore the committee.

Then I shall deal with voca-ional training. I believe I can make my point n that, without touching the other matters, 'he point is that these men of the merchant avy are not receiving the same training enefits as are the men of the other forces, ly submission is that they should be treated i exactly the same way. It has been sur-rising to read some of the statements made y members of the cabinet about these men.
For example, in January of this year the linister of Veterans Affairs was out at the
Supply-Transport
coast and, when he was asked about these merchant navy veterans, he said this:
We have gone so far in the field of veterans affairs without friction between civilians-
Note that word "civilians".
-and members of the armed forces, that to give special benefits to special groups would kill something good.
In effect he was saying that merchant navy veterans were civilians, and was distinguishing them from the members of the other three armed forces. That stand is very different from the statement contained in the speech from the throne at the close of the war. In the speech from the throne on September 6, 1945, we find this:
We rejoice that our armed forces have achieved so much in helping to defend and liberate nations to whose past and present our own is so closely akin. Our country will ever remember with pride the heroic exploits of Canada's fighting men and merchant seamen.
That was the attitude in 1945. Statements to that effect had been made by the former prime minister and, I think, by most of the ministers of that time, including no doubt the present Minister of Transport. So my suggestion is that on this question of, let us say, vocational training, these men should be treated in exactly the same way as the members of the other forces.
I raise this matter now because the other night the minister said that there is to be a supplementary vote covering this rehabilitation. Therefore it is not too late for him to give consideration to widening the scope of this vocational ' training. I am afraid the difficulty is that the Department of Transport has been looking at this training only from the point of view of training men who are going to stay in the merchant navy.
At page 54 of the 1949 report we find this:
The Department of Transport was authorized to take the necessary steps to implement the recommendation-
That is, for training.
-in such a way as not to induce merchant seamen to abandon the sea as a means of livelihood.
That was the approach of the minister's advisers, as indicated in this report, namely, that the training was to be given only in such a way that it would not induce sailors to abandon the sea as a means of livelihood. The result was, of course, that the benefits were very seriously curtailed.
For example there is the restriction that a man over thirty years of age cannot qualify for this vocational training unless special provision is made for him. His case is to be the exception, rather than the rule. I do not think there should be any age limit. If these men can benefit by vocational training, then they should be allowed to have

merchant seaman having obtained either one or other of the bonuses I mentioned a moment ago. If he did not get one of those two bonuses he is not entitled to vocational training under the orders in council.
What about the young men who were too young to sign manning pool contracts?
What about them?
Why are they not allowed to take this training?

I presume it is because they were too young to sign an agreement when they entered the merchant navy. My information is that there were very few who were unable to sign manning pool agreements. I do not know the age limit when war was declared, but I presume it was the legal age limit of eighteen years. There would be many men under that age who would be turned away and my information is that most of them went to serve with foreign merchant marines.
If a boy served on a Canadian ship even without signing a manning pool agreement, why should he not get the training?

The veterans affairs committee was charged with the responsibility of going into this whole matter two years ago. That committee made a number of recommendations and I believe that those concerning the merchant marine were approved by the government. The result of that approval was these two orders in council that have been referred to. My hon. friend asks why these men who were too young are not covered by the orders in council. I can give no other answer than that the veterans affairs committee received representations, heard evidence and brought down recommendations which the government accepted. Beyond that I do not think I can go.
I do not believe the veterans affairs committee received full representations on this point.
They certainly brought in a full report.

Even if they did, that was two or three years ago. Here we have the position that the responsibility is that of the Department of Transport. It had charge of all these men during the war years. I presume the department has a record of the men who served on Canadian ships whether or not they got a bonus. I suggest that if a man served on a Canadian ship he should at least be given an opportunity to take this training.
Supply-Transport What has his age got to do with it? A man who is thirty-five needs rehabilitation just as much as a younger man. Now that the minister has the information and is aware of the need for something to be done about it I urge upon him that further consideration be given to broadening the terms of the order in council.

With reference to the veterans affairs committee, I have not the report here but my recollection is that their recommendations were not all carried out by the department. We made a number of recommendations that received no consideration at all. I would not like the minister to be definite in saying that all the recommendations of the veterans affairs committee were carried out so far as the merchant marine is concerned.
I am not now and was not then a member of the veterans affairs committee but my officers inform me that all recommendations made concerning vocational training of merchant seamen were carried out.
We are both speaking without having the record here, but I am satisfied that the record will not bear out the minister's statement.

I have a copy of a telegram sent to the minister on May 20, I believe, by the Canadian merchant navy veterans association in which they imply that many hundreds of veterans had no way of learning about the vocational training benefits that were offered, and had no opportunity to see the advertisements placed by the department to which the minister referred on May 11. Has the minister any statement to make?

That telegram is entirely inaccurate and erroneous. I replied that there was plenty of opportunity for publication. Publication was made in the house, over the radio, and in a number of notices and advertisements. The hon. member for Halifax demanded on more than one occasion that the time limit be extended. So did the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra and other members of the house. They also asked for the extension of the age limit. There was plenty of publicity given to the matters referred to in that telegram.

Is there to be any provision made for the men who have been losing their jobs as a result of the policy announced last December? I have a press dispatch dated December 10, 1949, which appeared in one of the Vancouver papers. The heading is:
Beached Seamen Offered Training for Other Jobs

Supply-Transport
The article reads in part:
Five thousand Canadian seamen left "on the beach" by the government's order cutting the merchant marine will get vocational training.
That was the news which went out across the country last December 10. So far as I can see, absolutely nothing has been done along that line.

We are just getting into the position that you tried to avoid, Mr. Chairman, by your direction at the outset of this discussion. I would think the time to discuss the question of the men whose employment on the sea may be affected would be when we come to the item for the maritime commission or the item of $3 million subsidy provided following the statement made by the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister made a statement in December of last year in which he outlined the policy in respect of the transfer of ships, subsidies, and the like. That article certainly is not in accordance with the facts. Unfortunately some men will be put out of work. I will be able to deal with that when we come to it, but certainly the number is nowhere in the proximity of the figure given by my hon. friend.

Item agreed to.
Marine service-
468.	Marine service steamers, including icebreakers-maintenance, operation and repairs, $3,603,070.
I should like to know how many icebreakers there are in this service, where they operate as icebreakers, and during the season when .there is no ice in what capacity they are employed.

There are three icebreakers under this item, the Lapointe, the McLean and the Lady Grey. A new ship, the C. D. Howe, is being provided and she will be used in the dual capacity of icebreaker and for the transport of supplies to the northern part of the country. The other ships mentioned break ice in the wintertime, and at other times carry supplies to the eastern and Arctic areas, and to the various lighthouses and lighthouse depots on the east coast.
Will the minister tell the house the necessity for the increase of $502,000?

It is because of two new ships that are being brought into operation, the C. D. Howe, which I mentioned a moment ago) and the Edward Cornwallis. The Edward Cornwallis will operate from the Atlantic coast and the C. D. Howe from Quebec.
What company is building the C. D. Howel

The Davie Shipbuilding
Company.

Under this item I notice that the number of wireless operators has been increased from two to six. I am rather curious to know whether this indicates a change in policy on the part of the government as to the number of wireless operators that should be carried on our ships, and if the government is setting an example for other ship operators.

I would not say there is a change in policy. I think it is because of the new ships. With the construction of these vessels we intend to put into effect the most modern means of communication and transportation. That accounts for the increase in the number of operators.

These ships usually operate within a stone's throw of lighthouses, and most of the time they are close to radio stations. I would have thought you would be able to use ordinary radio telephone equipment.
The C. D. Howe and the McLean operate away up at Churchill and in the northeastern Arctic area, as will the Cornwallis.

I notice one detail in this item amounting to $1,163,626 involving 773 so-called temporary assistants for which no detail whatever is given. There is just the lump sum of over a million dollars. Is there any explanation?
This covers the personnel of the various ships.

Item agreed to.
Marine service-
469.	Construction, maintenance and supervision of aids to navigation, including salaries and allowances to lightkeepers, $4,503,495.
What bonuses have been given to lighthouse keepers, over and above their contracts, to take care of the high cost of living?

I think there is a misapprehension. For the most part lighthouse keepers operate under the civil service commission, and from time to time they get statutory increases and reclassifications. They would not be entitled to a bonus as such.

Item agreed to.
Marine service-
470.	Agencies-salaries and office expenses, $436,505.
There is an increase of $65,091 in this item. Would the minister explain it?
Yes. There are 102 annual increases, that is statutory increases varying from $5 to $10 per month. Then there are 147 basic- salary increases, which amount to $26,000.
Was there an increase in personnel?
Yes, because of the entry of Newfoundland into confederation.

Item agreed to.
Marine service-
471.	Maintenance and repairs to wharves, $5,000.

This item is said to be for the maintenance and repair of wharves, but the details show $1,500 for materials and supplies, $1,500 for travelling expenses and $2,000 for sundries. Where do the repairs come in?
Well, Mr. Chairman, this is a small item-
I know it is, but I want to know why they have to travel so much without doing any repairs.

If my hon. friend will permit I shall try to explain it. As the committee knows, the Department of Public Works is responsible for repairs to most of the wharves under the jurisdiction of the Department of Transport, but from time to time there are minor demands made by various 'bodies, organizations and groups; and before it can be determined whether or not the work should come under this vote a certain amount of travelling is necessary. That is the reason for the $1,500.
Then what are the sundries?
That is to cover long distance telephone calls and snow clearing.
Do I understand that the work is looked after by public works, and you supply the material?
No, we do not supply the materials.
Then what are these supplies for?
We do the work ourselves, in these small items.
Then there are no salaries or wages involved?
No.
How is the work done, then; by a miracle?
It is done by marine service employees, or other employees of the department. These are small repairs which amount to perhaps $50, $60 or $100.

Item agreed to.
Supply-Transport Marine service-
473. To provide for Canada's share of the cost of the North Atlantic ice patrol, $20,000.
What agency does the ice patrolling in the spring of the year? Is it the same one that is covered by this item for the North Atlantic ice patrol?

No, this is an entirely different matter. This is done by international agreement, among several countries, under the safety of life at sea convention which was signed in London in 1929 and re-negotiated in 1948. By virtue of that international agreement Canada is assessed a certain portion of the cost of patrolling the ice in the eastern area.

Item agreed to.
Marine service-
475.	Life-saving service, including rewards for saving life, $137,490.
Will the minister explain this item in which there appears to have been a substantial reduction?

As the committee will remember, last year a relatively large amount was voted to cover the acquisition of four lifeboats, two on the east coast and two on the west coast. It has been found possible to acquire only one of those, and we have not proceeded with the other three because of the reference to an interdepartmental committee of the matter of air rescue operations. There was no use spending money until it was known what the decision would be in that regard, and that is why there is a reduction.
What is the position now with respect to the air rescue reference?

I am afraid I cannot add anything to what I said the other day. Perhaps I should say that on two occasions I have had an opportunity of discussing the work of the committee with the chairman of the maritime commission, and I am hopeful that it will be possible to make an announcement soon.
Is there any possibility of Canada establishing a coastguard service in the near future?
I would not like to answer that until I am in a position to deal fully with the report.

Item agreed to.
Marine service-
476.	To provide subsidies for wrecking plants- Quebec and British Columbia, $65,000.
To what firms or persons are these moneys payable?

To the extent of $40,000 they are payable to the Quebec Salvage and Wrecking Company Limited, and to the

Supply-Transport
extent of $25,000 to Pacific Salvage Limited, to ensure that adequate facilities are provided both east and west in case of wrecks.
Is that paid on the basis of the work they do, or is it an annual retainer?
It is an annual contract.

Item agreed to.
Marine service-
478.	Miscellaneous services relating to navigation and shipping, including grants as detailed in the estimates; and for repayment to a proper authority, or to the government of the United Kingdom, under section 296 of the Canada Shipping Act, of expenses incurred in respect of distressed seamen left behind out of Canada, including the repayment of excepted expenses, as defined in the said section, $138,809.
Would the minister explain this item?

This is for the following miscellaneous activities related to navigation and shipping: examination of candidates for masters' and mates' certificates; operation of navigation schools at Yarmouth, Halifax, Saint John and Quebec for training candidates for certificates of competency; investigations into marine casualties; registration of shipping; removal of obstructions to traffic in navigable waters; grants in aid to separately operated schools of navigation at Rimouski, Kingston and Vancouver.
Do these examiners travel about, or do the examinations take place at certain definite points?
Both. Some examinations take place at the schools; others are conducted by examiners who travel from the office in Ottawa.

I notice that this item includes payments to the United Kingdom in connection with the repatriation of seamen to Canada, but I can find no reference to that in the details on page 295. Was any of this money spent for that purpose last year?
Yes, money was spent to repatriate from the United Kingdom and other parts of the world seamen who were stranded or otherwise in difficulty.
Has the minister any details of the amount spent for that purpose?
I am sorry I do not have them available. I will see that my hon. friend gets them.
According to the details I notice that the item for sundries has increased by some $18,000. Could the minister explain the reason for that increase?

The increase in sundries is made up as follows: An additional amount provided in this item for the removal of

obstructions to navigation. The previous vote of $5,000 was not sufficient for even a minor job of this nature. That accounts for $17,000. Then, there is an additional amount to cover the payment of charges incurred on account of excepted expenses, those relating to deserted seamen, $1,900. This answers, in part, the question asked by the member for York South.

Item agreed to.
Marine service-
479.	Steamship inspection and the carrying out of the provisions of the conventions for the safety of life at sea and load lines, $394,280.

Has the minister taken into consideration the inspection under the new rules which will be in force within a short time on all steamships, or is this item similar to the one covering inspections made under the provisions before the new regulations came into effect?
This is the same vote as before, and covers the same personnel, the same administrative operation.
It does not anticipate what will have to be done in the next year to make these ships safe?

No. Well, we do not spend money to make ships safe. The government passes regulations and it is the company that is affected by the regulations that spends the money. My answer was therefore correct, but I thought I should add that explanation.
There is quite a heavy item of travelling expenses here, an increase of over $4,000. Could the minister explain the reason for that?

If my hon. friend will recall, it was said in the last two years, and rightly so, that there was not a sufficient number of steamship inspections. There were nine additional inspectors appointed, and that accounts for the increase in travelling expenses.

There has been some talk during this session of adopting new regulations, for example with regard to the use of radio operators on ships. The minister has said that he would bring down amendments to the Canada Shipping Act. The session is now drawing to a close, and the house is starting morning sittings next week. I hope the minister can bring down those amendments fairly soon. Can he give us some indication as to when we may expect them?

I am as anxious as anyone to bring them down. I should point out to the house that it will be a rather lengthy bill, because it includes all the safety of life at sea conventions that were made at the conference in 1948. While it left my depart-

ment some time ago, it has to be approved by the Department of Justice. At this time the Department of Justice has a considerable number of bills, and other legislation that must be given consideration. I am hopeful that it will be possible to have it approved next week, but that does not mean it will be on the order paper next week. I hope it will be on the order paper early in June.
Is it still the intention of the government to put through the amendments at this session?
Yes, it is. I am most anxious to put them through.

Item agreed to.
Marine service-
480.	Marine signal service, $158,643.

I notice in this vote there is an item of $34,000 for telegrams, telephones and postage. This amount constitutes about one-flfth of the whole item. I believe that with the air mail service we have today the department could curtail some of these telegrams and telephone calls. I know it is handy when you have a telephone at your elbow to call Vancouver or Halifax, but under present circumstances I believe some of these expenditures could be drastically curtailed. The item seems to be the same as last year's, so could the minister tell me how much of the $34,000 was used last year?
All of it.
I think that is an item that could be curtailed.

Perhaps I should say to the hon. member that this covers the rental of various lines. The marine signal service is a service which operates on the St. Lawrence and in other parts of Canada, and must report as many as eight, ten, twenty or twenty-five times a day the passage of ships at certain points. It is a service using facilities rented from the telephone company.

Item agreed to.
Marine service-
481.	River St. Lawrence ship channel-contract dredging in the St. Lawrence river and Montreal harbour, including cost of administration-capital, $3,128,052.

This item appears every year, Mr. Chairman, as an expenditure of about $3 million. What class of dredging is being done-rock dredging or just mud digging? It seems to be a large item, and apparently the channel requires dredging every year.

This item covers a contract entered into between the government and Marine Industries Limited for the deepening and widening of the St. Lawrence ship channel, which extends from about forty miles below Quebec to the head of the Lachine
Supply-Transport
canal. It covers stone, gravel and the like. It is a contract which is now in its fourth year, and which provides for dredging to a certain depth, namely 35 feet, and the widening of the channel at certain portions, as well as provision for anchorage bases where ships can anchor at night and still be out of the channel.
It is for one contractor?
Yes.
Who is the contractor?
Marine Industries Limited.
What has been the total expenditure to date for dredging, deepening and widening the channel in the St. Lawrence?
I think I would have to get that information for the hon. member, if he will allow me. I have not got it here.
The minister said that this covers a contract, but the contract only accounts for a portion of the item. Why is it necessary to have a staff of 125 to look after this contract?

It is necessary, under the terms of the contract, to see to it that this work is done. We have the staff to make sure that the terms of the contract are being carried out; it is being checked, audited and so forth.
Are all the 125 people occupied in checking the contract?

They are on various ships. If my hon. friend had been down the St. Lawrence at this time of year, and more particularly in June and July, he would notice dredges extending from Montreal harbour right down to below Quebec. There are as many as five or six ships doing this work, and it is necessary to have a crew on each ship.

Is it not a contract with Marine Industries? The minister has said there is a contract with this company to do the dredging. Now, what work do the government officials do? Apparently there are 125 government officials, and the item is listed as covering contract dredging. What work do the 125 government officials do which makes up the balance of the item?

They prepare the plans and specifications, and tell these people what work they have to do; that is set out in the contract. Then, they supervise the work, and that includes the 125 men to whom my hon. friend refers.

Before this item passes, I should like to ask the minister the explanation of the note which appears on

Supply-Transport
page 297 of the estimates, "contract dredging -capital-$2,939,500." As I understand it, we are passing the annual appropriations for this service.
I do not understand that question.
On page 297 the minister will note in the details of this vote we are passing, "contract dredging-capital -$2,939,500." Then there is an item under it of maintenance, $300,000.
I am informed that is the cost of our own office, divided between capital and maintenance.
Are we voting now capital outlays on these annual estimates?
Yes. We are voting an amount of $2,939,500 which is a payment that will be made to this company for the dredging of the channel.
Are we making any appropriations out of annual expenditures for dredging or is it all borrowed money?
It is a payment under a contract for dredging.
We borrow the money to pay for it?
No, we do not borrow the money.
It is under capital. As I understand capital, it is borrowed money; it is capital expenditures.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Did the minister not give the wrong figure there?
It is to differentiate it between the amount paid the company and the other items that are set out in the details.

It is rather hard to understand that explanation. In the details we find "contract dredging, capital, $2,939,500; maintenance, $300,000." If it is a contract to do this work, why should that payment be divided into capital and maintenance? Just what is the reason? That terminology does not seem to fit the actual situation.

I think I get the point now. The capital is divided in accordance with the work that is done along the channel. For instance, the $2,939,500 is made up of an item of $970,000 in the Montreal harbour; $10,000 at Longue Pointe; $166,000 at Pointe aux Trembles channel; $681,000 in lake St. Peter at Yamachiche bend; $37,000 at Cap de la Madeleine; $10,000 at Becancour;

$450,000 at Cap a la Roche; $5,000 at Ste. Croix; $609,000 at Brule Bank channel. That is a breakdown of the capital amount of money paid to the contractor for the work along the channel extending from Montreal to Quebec.
Why is it called capital? Because apparently this money has to be spent every year. It certainly does not look like a capital item as we understand the word.

This is a five-year contract. This is work for one year only. According to the terms of the contract the work must be completed within a period of five years and they do about a fifth. They have the right to do a little more each year if they wish. The amount that they will do in 1950-51 is the amount as I have just read it.
Next year they will do a different part of the river, is that right?
Next year they will do a different part of the river.
What does this maintenance mean? There is $300,000 for maintenance. How does that enter into the picture?
That item is our own expenditure. It is to cover stone lifters and other ships of the Department of Transport that are used in conjunction with the operation and completion of this contract.

So that, in addition to the contract, the government spends $300,000 for maintaining its own equipment, also engages 125 employees and then has other items such as board, $48,250; fuel, $66,000; materials and supplies, $32,000; repairs and upkeep of equipment, $70,000; and sundries, $11,463. Those are all government items over and above what is paid to this firm under the contract. Is that right?
The item of $2,939,500 is the item that I gave the breakdown for a moment ago. I am informed that the other items are expenditures of our own department.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Expenditures of the minister's own department for doing what? From the estimates it looks as though they are expenditures in administering the expenditure of the $2,939,500 and the $300,000.

I indicated a moment ago that there was an engineering staff in the department that prepares the plans and specifications and that lays out each year the work that must be done under the contract; and the items are set out in the details.
The minister has mentioned several localities where dredging is being done. Is that all under one contract?
Yes.
It is all under one contract, the minister says. Were there different tenders called for this on a five-year undertaking or five-year contract?
There is just one tender called for, or rather there is just one contract. There were several tenders, if my recollection serves me aright, although it is four or five years ago now.

What is the explanation of this item at the bottom of the detail:
Less: Amount chargeable to administration, maintenance and operation, $628,505.
How does that credit arise?
That is the amount that goes into the next vote: amount chargeable to administration, maintenance and operation.
It goes into the vote next year, you mean?
No; into the next item, item 482.

Item agreed to.
Marine service-
483. To provide towards the construction of an icebreaking vessel to meet the St. Lawrence and northern transportation requirements (estimated cost $5,000,000) capital (revote $400,000), $2,000,000.

Just where is this icebreaker being constructed and were tenders called? Are bigger and heavier icebreakers being built with the object in view of opening the channel of the St. Lawrence river earlier every spring? I understand that this was one of the purposes of building icebreakers, and I should like to hear from the minister whether that is correct or not.

As to the last question, it is rather difficult to answer it categorically or specifically, because it is the hope that the St. Lawrence will be opened up to navigation earlier each year, but that hope is not always met.
At that point may I ask the minister if he considers that this object is altogether fair to the maritime ports of Saint John and Halifax?

I do not think that it is unfair to them. The icebreakers do a job not only with reference to the opening of the port but, as my friend knows, also one that has a great deal to do with avoiding flood conditions. Each year in the spring in the Laprairie basin on the south side of the river St. Lawrence in the Montreal area there is a backing of ice which causes a great deal of damage. Experience has taught us in the department that the more quickly we can get
Supply-Transport
the channel opened and break the ice, the less danger there is of a backing of water. Some two or three years ago serious damage was done to both sides of the Jacques Cartier bridge. Certainly it is not done with the object of hurting in any way the maritime ports. On the contrary, the national harbours board does everything in its power by way of making available additional facilities to assist the ports. The Department of Transport has provided a number of new ships. The Edward Cornwallis has been launched and is now in operation, and there is provision for other ships for the maritimes.

But opening the port of Montreal and taking trade- away from the ports of Saint John and Halifax does not in any way help the maritime ports. I can understand the use of an icebreaker to do away with the condition the minister mentioned in connection with the flooding of the channel, and the danger from ice; but I do not follow his other argument.
I presume this is for the building of a new member in the icebreaker fleet. What is the definition of the term "northern" as it is found in the estimate?
The purpose of this icebreaker is to service the ports in the northeastern Arctic. It is to break the ice in the St. Lawrence, and from time to time replace the McLean in that area.

Since the minister has expressed the hope that the St. Lawrence river might be opened up, I was going to express the hope that the same thing might happen with the Hudson bay route. To what extent have icebreakers which have been used on the St. Lawrence gone into northern waters under their own steam for icebreaking purposes?
They are sent up north each year. The McLean makes an annual trip to the northeastern Arctic, and into Hudson bay to Churchill.

I know about the McLean.
Has any other ship gone up there in recent years?
The C. D. Howe will make a journey up there.
It will blast things out.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: That will get rid of the ice, especially the thin ice.
The minister did not answer my question as to where this new icebreaker was being built, and also whether tenders were being called.

The Davie Shipbuilding Company.

Supply-Transport
In Glasgow?
No, at Lauzon, Quebec.
Is that the new aluminum icebreaker?
No.
Were tenders called for construction, and what were the amounts of those tenders.
No, tenders were not called for.
Is that considered good business?

I think it is, under the circumstances. Perhaps I could explain to the committee why that was done. The experience in the Department of Transport two years back was that when tenders were called some yards that were deserving of work were not able to get it because they were never the lowest tenderers. I do not wish to mention the names of any yards, but I know of one, which is very efficient, and to which many of the tenders were going.
Representations were made to us that that was not a fair method of procedure, and that if the Department of Transport and the government were going to build ships they should be divided as fairly as possible among the main yards. We acceded to that request and instructed the maritime commission to prepare a plan whereby the main shipyards of this country would be awarded contracts for the vessels required for the Department of Transport and other departments. By virtue of that policy I think a fair distribution has been made.
I have not the total items now, but I think I can give pretty substantial reasons for indicating why that was good policy.
Then how did the department arrive at the amount that should be paid for the construction of these icebreakers and [DOT]other vessels, if no tenders are called?

The maritime commission and the department were given the responsibility of making estimates of the cost of the ship. In some cases the tenders were [DOT]called but not accepted; and in some cases contracts were granted on a cost-plus basis.
In this instance these ships were costing more money than they should; is that right?
No, they are not.
This one ship may cost much more. You do not know whether it is higher or lower than it should be. It definitely must be more.
I am saying it is not.
How do you know? You have no method of finding out.
Yes, I told the hon. member.
The commission does not know.
Oh, yes, they do; and probably the hon. member would be one of the first to admit that, after a while, when we come to another item.
Which one?
We will see.
Tell me now.
The commission has a staff, and so has the Department of Transport.
Are they naval engineers?

3ome of them are. And they are able to establish the costs of the ships. Furthermore there is the auditing branch, treasury officers, not only in the Department of Transport, but in the Department of Finance, that supervises the operation of these contracts.
All they would do is this: when accounts would come to them they would check them and pass them. They would not check items to see whether purchases could be made cheaper somewhere else.

It seems to me that in his explanation the minister definitely said that certain shipyards-or that a certain shipyard -were getting the greater part of the work, because their tenders were consistently lower. He seemed to indicate that one shipyard was getting most of the work. Then representations were made that this was not fair, and it was as a result of those representations that the policy was instituted of dividing up the work among the various shipyards.
It seems to me that if that is the basis of the new policy-and I believe I have reproduced correctly what the minister said- then the only result can be that the cost of building these ships is going to be greater, because instead of tenders being given to the shipyard which consistently made the lowest tenders, they are given to other shipyards without calling for tenders at all. I do not believe any other conclusion can be drawn from the minister's explanation. While we are on this subject I suggest the minister should tell us who is building this particular ship, and how many naval architects there are on the maritime commission?

Mr. Chairman, just to recapitulate what I said: Early in 1949 the government reached the conclusion that, from the

national defence point of view, and following out the recommendation made in the report of the Canadian 'maritime commission, it was imperative to maintain in operation a nucleus of shipyards for construction purposes. It directed the maritime commission to determine, in so far as the government ship construction program was concerned, which yards* should be given the work, in order to help them maintain a minimum of employment in their yards.
My hon. friends often complain about the fact that certain shipyards do not get contracts. That complaint has been made in the House of Commons from time to time. The attempt here was to meet the request which had been made. As a result of this policy a number of necessary government ships are at the present time being built, the major orders being as follows: naval icebreaker, Marine Industries Limited, Sorel, Quebec; Department of Transport icebreaker, Davie Shipbuilding, Lauzon, Quebec.
What are the figures?

I am now dealing with item 483. I can give further information when we come to the other vote. Item 483 makes provision for $5 million. Then, these further ships: three naval escort vessels, Vickers, Montreal; Burrards, Vancouver; and Halifax Shipyards, Halifax; two weather ships for the Department of Transport, Marine Industries Limited, Sorel; Gate vessel, George T. Davie, Levis, Quebec; four minesweepers, Saint John drydock, Davie shipbuilding, Port Arthur shipyard and Victoria machinery depot.
So far as the cost is concerned, before we build these ships we have the advice of independent naval architects. In the case of the ship we are discussing we had the advice of German and Milne who gave an estimate of what it would cost to build a ship. We proceeded on the same basis when we built the S.S. Abegweit. The Abegweit was built on a cost-plus basis, but before we decided to build it we obtained from the same firm of naval architects, German and Milne, an estimate of the cost. We are proceeding on the same basis in connection with item 483.
That does not tell us anything.
When was the contract let?
The contract has not been signed.

There is a note in the item, "estimated cost, $5,000,000; capital revote, $400,000." In the details it is shown that under this item in 1949-50 the sum of $1 million was authorized. I was wondering how
Supply-Transport
this amount could get into the estimates last year and how there could be a revote such as is mentioned this year?
That was provided in the further supplementary estimates, 1949-50. It takes some time to prepare plans and specifications.
But $1 million, surely not?

This is an estimate, it is not a case of voting money that has been contracted for. In this case the total cost of the ship is estimated to be $5 million and we are putting in the estimates an item of $2 million. In last year's supplementary estimates we had an item of $1 million, but it was not possible to advance the progress of the plans and specifications sufficiently to enter into a contract. The same applies this year. The plans and specifications are in course of preparation but they are not sufficiently advanced to permit the signing of a contract. They will be during the course of the year and that is why the amount is in there.
Will these new icebreakers be able to break ice in Hudson bay?

That is a difficult question to answer because it would depend a great deal on the thickness of the ice. In so far as the N. B. McLean is concerned, it has always been successful in getting to Churchill, sometimes under very adverse conditions, it having had some narrow escapes. This icebreaker will be more modern and I think should be stronger than the McLean.
How will the new boat compare with the S.S. Abegweit? Will it be as powerful and will it do the same class of icebreaking?

No, she will not do the same class of icebreaking. This is not the same kind of ship. The Abegweit was built as a ferry boat to operate between Prince Edward Island and the mainland and to break ice at certain seasons of the year. This ship is not in the same class. It is not going to cost as much but I suppose it will be a more modern ship.
Will she have a greater horsepower than the Abegweit?
She is to have 10,800 horsepower and may go to a maximum of 14,000.

As I understand it, we authorized $1 million in last year's supplementary estimates, but this year we are being asked to authorize $2 million, of which $400,000 is a revote. That would indicate that we spent $600,000 of the money authorized last year.

Supply-Transport
If I am incorrect in my understanding I ask the minister to tell us what was spent last year.
We spent $40,000.
Why is there only a revote of $400,000 of what was authorized last year? Why is not the revote $960,000?
I must confess that I cannot explain it. I am told that all we spent was $40,000, and that was spent in the preparation of plans and specifications.
To what extent is the St. Lawrence season lengthened by the use of icebreakers?
I am informed that it is difficult to give an exact estimate. They do help to hasten the opening of navigation but the main purpose is to prevent flooding.
At about what date in the spring would the need for icebreakers cease?
It varies from year to year. I think this year it was April 10; I have known it to be in March, and some years it is the end of April.
The fact that the St. Lawrence is open so much earlier than Churchill should make available to Churchill all the necessary icebreaking equipment when the season there is about to open.

To a large extent that is right, but one must keep in mind that a ship cannot get up to Churchill at all seasons in the year. If navigation is open here about April 10 I would think it would be difficult for the McLean or any other icebreaker to operate in the Hudson bay area at that time. If my hon. friend wants me to say that with the additional icebreakers more will be available for that area, I think the answer would be "yes."
May I suggest to the minister that they could go up there a little earlier than they have been going up.
Why should they go up at all?
They certainly could go up there in May or June.

I think this item should stand. Going back to what the minister said a moment ago, we were told that only $40,000 was spent last year when we authorized $1 million. Instead of being told that the revote this year is $960,000, it is only $400,000. This year we are being asked to authorize $2 million and it does not seem possible to reconcile the explanations. Would it not be wiser to let this item stand until a full explanation can be given? If we are in fact

revoting $960,000 of what was authorized last year, not only should that be made known to the committee but it is possible that the $2 million we are being asked to authorize this year could be reduced accordingly. When the minister is dealing with that could he tell us when this contract will be signed and how long it is expected it will take to build this icebreaker?

In explanation of the first question asked, I am told that when these estimates now before us were prepared it was anticipated that expenditures last year would amount to $600,000 leaving a revote of $400,000 out of the $1 million voted last year. I think that covers the point. The type of contract covering this icebreaker has not yet been decided upon. Therefore I am not able to answer the question. I do not know whether it will be a management fee contract, a cost plus contract, or perhaps a firm price contract although I have some doubt that it will be. I am informed that the time it will take to build the ship will be roughly a year and a half to two years.

Personally I am opposed to voting $2 million for a contract which is not yet signed. Not only has it not been signed but we have just been told that we do not know exactly what kind of contract we are going to have. Apparently it is quite a serious matter to decide just what the terms of the contract will be. It has been under negotiation for over a year now, and I would gather from what the minister has just said there are not any signs that it is nearing completion yet if all these other things remain to be decided. When our total expenditures are running so high I see no purpose in voting twice as much this year as we voted last year when we actually spent only $40,000 of what was voted. I do not see why the minister cannot get along with a million dollar vote this year.

If my hon. friend's argument is correct we will have to take out of the estimates at least five or six similar vessels. I am looking at the next page, not because I want to refer to it particularly, but there is an item to provide for the construction of an auto ferry between Yarmouth and a port in the New England states. When I made a statement in the house as to this project it received unanimous approval. That money is in the same position as item 483. The contract has not been let and the contract cannot be let for reasons that I will give when we come to the item. That applies to the weather ships and also to the ship on the east coast which are in these estimates. If my hon. friend's argument were to be followed we would never get anything done.

I am told the same thing applies to all these ships which I mentioned a moment ago. We want for the navy three naval escort vessels, a minesweeper and a gate vessel. We want a naval icebreaker for the navy, and if that argument were followed we would not get them at all.
Make no mistake about it, the Department of Finance gives all these things a pretty good check, and all departments get a pretty tough ride before treasury board when we ask for more than we are entitled to. The reason the amount is asked for is that it is anticipated that during the course of the year we will spend that money. We may not have to spend it. The reason we did not spend the $1 million we got last year was that the plans and specifications were not forthcoming nearly as quickly as we expected they would be, because of certain new technical developments in the field of icebreakers. I hope my hon. friend will not pursue his argument because it would cause some of his good friends on that side of the house to lose vessels which I am sure they would not want to lose, and which I am sure the people in those areas want to have.

That argument does not follow at all. What I have said is that we are faced with a contract which is not even signed yet, and we are being asked to vote $2 million for it. No assurance is given that the money will be required this year. In the case of the other vessels, if we could be assured that there is a good chance the money will be required this year then we would be willing to vote it, but if the situation is the same as the minister has indicated with respect to this contract then I am not sure, although we all agree that the contracts should be let and construction should proceed, that we should be required to vote large sums of money in advance of the signing of the contracts or in advance of a reasonable prospect that the contracts will be signed.

I am giving my hon. friend that assurance now. For instance, with reference to the Yarmouth ferry, the maritime commission and others are working on the plans and specifications, and if we do not get the $1 million involved there, and the $2 million under the item now before the committee, I would be the first one to be criticized because we were not moving fast enough. If I followed the argument of my hon. friend, then when I came back next year I would be asked why we did not move more rapidly and I would have to say "Oh well, the hon. member for Kamloops said that since the contract was not
Supply-Transport
signed we should not have the money in the estimates." I do not want to be unfair or derogatory but the position is a ridiculous one.
It certainly is, a revote of $400,000 and you tell us you only spent $40,000.

If my hon. friend understands me, the position taken by him is a ridiculous one. The proof of it is that work in this particular case has been started, and quite often contracts are not given prior to the voting of the money. I think that is a natural position to take.
Why do they start work before a contract is signed? Does that not prejudice the making of a proper contract?
I do not think it does. They have a letter of intention to proceed. That practice is not uncommon.

In what other departments of
the government is a practice of that kind followed?
By virtue of the statement I made and the policy I announced a moment ago, it is being followed in the case of all these ships.
Do I understand as to this revote of $400,000 there was $550,000 paid out for construction that has taken place so far?
No.
I may be dense but I do not understand this revote of $400,000. You say there was only $40,000 spent for plans. I cannot get it through my head. I do not see why that is in there at all.

I do not prepare the estimates. The Department of Finance arranges them. The explanation I gave a moment ago to the hon. member for Kamloops was that when these estimates were prepared last year it was anticipated that the expenditures last year would amount to $600,000 leaving a revote of $400,000 out of the $1 million voted last year.
But there was only $40,000 spent.
That is right.
When were the estimates prepared?
The main estimates were prepared in November, 1949.

Because it would appear that the situation is that the completion of a contract has not been possible at as early a date as was expected by the department, and

Supply-Transport
therefore the amount of money is not required that it was thought would be required. Is that the position?
That happens from time to time.
I can understand that but is the minister sure that in the present fiscal year he will require this $2 million?
Yes, I am.
In order that the contract may be proceeded with.
As much as any person can be sure, I am.

There is one thing about the whole picture that worries me quite a bit, and that is whether there is any method of keeping the price down to a fair figure. The minister will remember that during the war there was some provision-I am not sure whether or not it was in the contracts- whereby after ships had been built the department of munitions and supply went back and checked the costs very carefully, and I believe in many cases large amounts had to be paid back. The minister will know whether I am correct in that statement. Is a course of that kind to be followed here? I urge that some such plan be put into effect because otherwise these costs may just run wild. It seems to me where the government is letting these contracts without tenders there must be the most careful check, and also wide power to cut down the figure asked after the work has been done and it is possible to audit all the expenses. Is it the intention to have a contract of that type?

During the war-I am familiar with it because I had to make a special study of it-in the war expenditures committee we did examine various kinds of contracts. We came to the conclusion that fixed price contracts were of course the best; but we had to derogate from that practice on many occasions, and the next best was the cost plus percentage contract, the cost plus management fee contract, and various other kinds of bonuses added to the cost plus contract. During those days there was a renegotiation branch of the department of munitions and supply, which had auditors of its own together with those of treasury; and when it was discovered that costs were greater than they should be certain amounts of money were renegotiated. I am told that a similar procedure of renegotiation will be followed in all these contracts.
Has the minister the facilities in his department for carrying on renegotiations?

I am told that is to be done by the comptroller of the treasury.
[Mr. Green.1
Has the minister power under existing legislation to enter into contracts of that kind? I doubt very much whether there is that power.

I am told that these contracts contain a clause which is equivalent to renegotiation. In other words if the costs are higher than they should have been, there will have to be a renegotiation or a repayment after audit.

Has any consideration been given to following a tender system and then paying subsidies in order to help out the yard the government believes should have the work? The tender system would at least provide a check on the figures. The present arrangement appears to be a subsidy, in effect; that is what it amounts to. These firms which cannot build ships as cheaply as some other firms are getting the work at an increased price, so actually the government is paying a subsidy on at least some of these ships. Has any consideration been given to the use of tenders plus subsidies?
No.
Would anything of that kind be feasible?
I am informed that it would not be. I am told by one of the officers that the position then would be even worse than it is now.	.

The minister told the committee that he was being protected in letting these contracts without tenders through the estimates of firms of naval architects; and he mentioned one firm, German and Milne, who gave the department an estimate when the ferry Abegweit was under construction. Would the minister inform the committee what was the estimated cost of this boat, and what was the ultimate cost?

Yes, it will be.
Has the contract been let?

Can the plans be completed, the contract let, and $200,000 worth of work done within the fiscal year?

What firm is going to do this job?

Is it not unusual that we should be asked to vote money before we even know whai firm is going to do the work?

this item?

What firm built that boat?

Company.

486.	To provide towards the construction of an auto-ferry vessel for service between Yarmouth, N.S., and the New England states (estimated cost $3,000,000), subject to an agreement being entered into on the part of the province of Nova Scotia for a contribution, upon such terms and conditions as the governor in council may determine, up to 50 per cent of the cost of construction but not exceeding $1,500,000-capital, $1,000,000.

I should like the minister to make a statement with respect to
Supply-Transport
this item. This is the ferry being built to accommodate tourists between southern Nova Scotia and the state of Maine. I understand that fifty per cent of the cost is to be paid by the province of Nova Scotia. Would the minister make a statement?
What was the question?
I should like to know from the minister what progress is being made in the construction of the ferry to serve tourist traffic between southern Nova Scotia and the state of Maine.
As announced to the house some time ago, the government decided to defray one-half the cost of construction of a ferry vessel between Yarmouth and a point in the state of Maine.
Has that point been decided yet?

I will come to that. Eastern Steamship Lines, which operated the service, indicated to the maritime commission last year that they would not operate it after this season. So, after consultation with the government of Nova Scotia it was decided that each government would defray one-half the cost of construction, and a committee was set up to deal with the project. That committee was composed of C.N.R. officials, transport officials, maritime commission men, and I think someone from finance, together with representatives of Nova Scotia. This committee has met on several occasions. It is they who will decide the nature and type of the vessel. I believe that has been pretty well decided; and they will also decide the port at which the ship will call on the American side. That is still under discussion.
Who will operate the ship?
The Canadian National Railways, I hope.

Item agreed to.

487.	Repairs and expenses in connection with the operation and maintenance of official railway cars under the jurisdiction of the department, $64,000.

Mr. Chairman, I was going to ask how many private railway cars are involved in this expenditure. Is this to cover the repair or reconditioning or air-conditioning of one of the cars, which was not air-conditioned heretofore?

No, it is not. This covers the cost of operation, maintenance, running repairs and general overhaul of five official railway cars, two of which are the cars of the governor general; one is the car of the Prime Minister; one the car which is assigned to

Is the car which was formerly used by Mr. Mackenzie King now air-conditioned?

488.	Hudson Bay Railway-construction and improvements-capital. $35,000.
What is this expenditure for?

It is for capital expenses. Each year there are two votes concerning the Hudson Bay railway, one to cover capital expenditure and the other to cover the deficit of the railway. This covers: first, the construction of four new standard section houses between Amery and Churchill, $16,000; second, material, 40,000 rail anchors, $16,000; third, provision for contingencies, $2,000; fourth, engineering supervision, $1,000.

Item agreed to.
Railway service-
489.	Hudson Bay Railway-to provide for the difference between the expenditures for operation and maintenance and revenue accruing from operation during the year ending March 31, 1951, not exceeding $400,000.

I notice there is a reduction of $100,000 in this item over that of a year ago. We are all glad to see that reduction, although I do not know what brings it about. It may be due to better operation of the route during the last season, or it may be due to a more optimistic outlook for the handling of grain through the port in the coming year. Those of us who come from the west are looking forward to the day when an item such as this will not be necessary. I am sure we feel that if the fullest possible use could be made of the port this item would disappear from the estimates.
We have a very short season in that part of the country, but the season we do have is not being used to the fullest extent. The 1949 official season was about 65 days. During 20 of those days there was not a single ship in the harbour; for 27 days there was only one ship at a time, and for 18 there was more than one. If we are to have an economic use of this port, it is only reasonable that it be used to the fullest possible extent. We have the railway and the port facilities and I should like to see them used as much

as possible. It is my understanding that the men who are sent there to help in the operation of the facilities have to be paid whether or not they are working. Those of us who are from the west are greatly concerned about the Hudson bay route, and we look forward to seeing it used to the fullest possible extent.

May I ask the minister what use is to be made of the port this year? I saw a statement the other day by Mr. Dalgleish of the Dalgleish Lines to the effect that, while it was expected there would be more freight incoming this year, the difficulty was in getting cargoes for the outward bound ships. I quite agree with the member for Prince Albert, and the other members from the west, that we are all anxious to see proper use made of this port. The Hudson bay route association in western Canada has been doing everything in its power to get business for that port. It has never had a really thorough tryout, but many of us believe it is an economically feasible proposition from the point of view of the western grain producer, and particularly if the grain were there so that the ships could be loaded.
We need to encourage two-way traffic. While there has been a considerable increase in the amount of freight brought in, we do not want to see the outgoing ships without cargo, or ships not coming in, as is the case with the Dalgleish line who used that port for some years. Could the minister tell us something about the provisions for this year?

To deal first with the question of the hon. member for Prince Albert, the reason for the decrease in the deficit is an increase in the revenue. I am happy to say that business was much better than expected.
Dealing with the question of the member for Rosetown-Biggar I am unfortunately not able to tell him how much wheat will be moved out of Churchill. It is difficult to do that at this time. I can say though that in the last four years there has been a considerable increase. In 1946-47, the number of bushels moved was 1 million. It rose in the last fiscal year to 5,719,000 bushels. I hope the increase will continue this year.
Does the minister know what grain is in storage in the elevator ready for shipment?

I could not say, but I could get that information. I can deal with it when we come to the national harbours board item concerning the port of Churchill. It really is the item which concerns the elevator, not the railway.
All right.
It is true that the difficulty about Churchill is that there is outgoing cargo, but there is no incoming cargo.
It doubled last year.

Yes, but you will be interested in knowing that representations were made by the Hudson bay route association, which saw the Prime Minister and others quite recently. Because of the representations which were made by them, I made the announcement in the house which I think will be very helpful. I hope it will be possible, from time to time, [DOT] to assist this group, because I am sure the house would like to see more business directed through Churchill.
While this route is being considered, I may say that I do not see any estimate covering the survey of the Lynn lake route for the Hudson Bay railway. Is anything being done about that this year?
No, this matter just deals with the operation of the Hudson Bay railway itself. Any item covering a branch line, if there is to be one, would be in a supplementary estimate.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to join with my colleagues of the various political parties from the west in saying that I am very pleased now at the increased amount of activity there seems to be about the port of Churchill.
You have some Liberal members down here now.

I may say to the hon. member, as this house and the minister well know, I have been talking about this thing for the last five years; that would be my answer.
There is no doubt that grain is beginning to move towards the port of Churchill-a great deal earlier this year than it has before. As a matter of fact, my own estimate is that it is about a month earlier. As I say, I have been making speeches on this subject at various times; in fact, I made one earlier this session. I do not want to repeat what I said before. I was interested in the minister's statement that the reason there was a lower deficit was that there was more revenue. I may point out the self-evident fact that if still more use is made of the port there will be a still smaller deficit; that is the thing for which we have been pleading for years. It has been proven, I believe, that 15 million bushels passing over that route would cancel out the deficit, and after that we might even expect a small amount of profit.
I should like to thank the minister for his support, and particularly for the support which the government has given and the assurances given to the delegation which 55946-182
Supply-Transport
came down here. I may say that a member of that delegation came from my own city of Saskatoon. I think it was Mr. Woodward who presented the case to the government and who was for many years editor of our local paper there. I think a tribute should be paid here, if it is paid to any man; if this port ever does fulfil the expectations which some of us have for it, I think it will be largely due to the efforts of Mr. Frank Eliason, the present secretary of the Hudson bay route association; he is a man who has served that association under its various names but always with the one purpose in mind, namely that our people of the prairie west should make more use of the port that they have at their own back door.

491. Strait of Canso-transportation improvements and facilities-capital (revote $200,000), $2,000,000.

Before this item carries I should like a statement up to date from the minister advising us just what progress has been made with respect to drawing up the plans of the Canso bridge and the letting of the tenders. The public in Nova Scotia have for years been anxious to secure this bridge and they have accepted the assurances from the minister and the government that progress was being made with this undertaking and that the contract would be called for early this year. This calling for contracts was delayed, and the explanation was given by the minister and the premier of Nova Scotia; and notwithstanding the disappointment over the delay, the public in Nova Scotia have accepted the statement of the minister but they would like to know that the project is being proceeded with at an early date.

I do not know whether my hon. friend was in the house when some weeks ago I made a statement concerning a new development that had taken place. It was owing to the fact that the original plans were based on a roadway of twenty-two feet, but when discussions were entered into between the government and the provinces with regard to the trans-Canada highway, it was decided that the minimum width of that highway should be twenty-four feet. Hence certain revisions had to be made on the Canso project. I saw Dr. Pratley quite recently; he is the engineer in charge. He was one of the members of the board who recommended the low level bridge, and he is our consulting engineer in connection with the project. He is the one who is preparing the plans and specifications. He

Supply-Transport
informed me that these plans and specifications are now almost complete. He has already entered into discussions with the engineers of the Canadian National Railways and of the province of Nova Scotia, and will continue those discussions. Those plans that are now in the course of preparation and almost complete must of course be approved by the engineers of the government of Nova Scotia, of the Canadian National Railways and the board of transport commissioners. I presume the plans will have to be in their hands for some time before they receive final approval. But just as soon as they have been approved by those three groups of engineers Dr. Pratley assures me that he will then be in a position to call for tenders.
Can the minister indicate more definitely when he expects that the tenders will be called for?

I would say about August; but that again, of course, is subject to the time that the engineers will want to give to the study of the plans. I make this additional point. This is a particularly difficult project. Hon. members will recall the difficulty that there was from the point of view of the board of engineers and the discussion that was held, my own officers being of a certain view and the board of engineers being of another view. I should not like to be tied down to August, although I hope it will be then.

I realize that it is a difficult undertaking and that we have reliable engineers dealing with it. In this connection I should like to ask the minister if any progress is being made in the construction of the approaches of the bridge on both sides, on the Nova Scotia side and on the Cape Breton Island side.
No. I do not think it would be wise to touch this until the plans and specifications have been approved by both groups of engineers.

May I say that I was hoping that tomorrow we might go to item 524 of the transport estimates in order that there might be some discussion of freight rates in the house. prairies, in the maritimes and in British Columbia.
Mr. Speaker, there are about ten or twelve items still left unpassed before we get to the item of the board of transport commissioners.
The only thing is this. It would seem that we have been dealing with railways. This is a railway item, and the item that was to stand just now dealt with air service.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: There are over twenty items.
There are over twenty items between.
Twenty-six items.

I should like to get on with these items. Suppose we let the matter stand until six o'clock tomorrow and see what happens after that. Since my hon. friend spoke to me, others have said that while they are willing to have a debate on the decision of the board of transport commissioners as handed down today, they feel they should be given time to consider the effect of the decision, and that they would not have an opportunity of doing that if the debate were brought on tomorrow. I am in the hands of the house, ready to go on at three o'clock tomorrow. But I should like to go on until six o'clock with these estimates-

That would mean nine
o'clock tomorrow night, and it would give only two hours. I can understand that some hon. members might like to consider the report. But I do not like to see the House of Commons prevented from discussing this by, we will say, the fact that an appeal may be lodged-and undoubtedly if there is going to be an appeal it will be made within a few days.

The only appeal there can be is to the governor in council, and I think Mr. Speaker has already ruled that an appeal to the governor in council does not prevent the House of Commons from discussing the judgment.
Well, if that is so-

I am not quite sure about that; but that is my memory on the point. I believe that was the ruling by Mr. Speaker. The reason he prevented discussion before was that it was a review of the previous order. I certainly will not object to a discussion.	*
Then it is agreeable to the minister to go on after six o'clock tomorrow night? We could get along for a time.

I do think it would be better if it were set aside for another day.
Business of the House

I know there are those who would like an opportunity to examine the decision of the board of transport commissioners. If this item could be stood over until, let us say, Monday afternoon, then those who wish to discuss the matter would know in advance that it is to be dealt with and would have had an opportunity to examine the findings of the board of transport commissioners.

I am quite agreeable to any arrangement. I must point out however that next week I shall hardly be able to be here.
I have a commitment for the international trade fair on Monday; then ICAO sits on Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday, and I must be there. The earliest day for me next week would be Friday. That is the only day I would have available.

If the minister would just name a day, it would not matter which day. Let there be a day set aside for this. I would be agreeable to that, because I am interested in it. If the minister wishes to make it Thursday or Friday of next week, that would be all right.
Friday would be all right with me, if it would be agreeable to the house.
So long as we are not delaying it too long. That is the only point that worries me.
Friday would be all right.

Of course, unless my estimates could be moved forward to the point where we would come to the item for the board of transport commissioners early tomorrow-under those circumstances it would be all right.
I do suggest that this matter is of sufficient importance that it would be desirable if at all possible to let members have an opportunity of examining the findings before the discussion takes place.
So long as they do not delay too long, and the rates are put into effect, or something of that kind.
Then, let us say Friday.
They have to publish a tariff.
There is an allowance of fifteen days. It would be within the fifteen, days if we had it next Friday.
I would agree to next Friday.
Then, let us leave it at Friday, subject to an appeal for an earlier date being made, if something of an urgent nature comes up.

That is satisfactory.
